#6295. My Abysmal Enterprise Car Rental Experience In Omaha

Attending to a personal matter in Omaha with little notice, I booked a flight, hotel, and car rental. The miracle of points and miles is the ability to make anything happen when you really need it to without significant expense or inconvenience and I recommend to anyone that asks me about the loyalty space to leave a reserve to of 2.5x standard rates for an emergency trip home.

The flight was unremarkable (and priced about at that range, unfortunately), the hotel was a remodeled but otherwise unremarkable Hampton Inn, well located for my visit. But my typical rental car provider, National (owned by ERAC) was unavailable at the airport. I have some status with Avis and Hertz due to credit cards and reciprocal status but wanted to try the Drive Alliance angle for Enterprise companies. However, this required a nearby city location and not an airport rental. Honestly, it wasn’t that big of a deal to grab a Lyft to the downtown location at 23rd & Harney, and because of a credit, the ride only set me back $6.97 before tip.

Upon arrival, I was informed that my preferred car type was unavailable. For my trip a few vehicle types were offered, the cheapest being a mystery vehicle, but I opted for 2-4 levels above that for a Standard car and paid more for it. Not only was I told that the car I paid more for was not available, but that they only had minivans and there were zero other choices.

“Car choices aren’t guaranteed when booking within 24 hours.” There’s a little more context due, I know that car types are never guaranteed, but typically there’s more than just one type left.

“I don’t see that on my confirmation, can you show it to me?” She couldn’t, of course, then stated that “St. Louis”, ERAC headquarters, isn’t connected to their inventory. This opens a host of other questions. I searched the website, then I tried Google, then I enlisted AI and none of those options showed me specific adjustments described by the branch attendant stated by ERAC specific to the 24-hour booking period. I reached out to the brand on October 20th, it has yet to respond.

I had a choice to make, either take what they have or move on. As I was not at the airport and couldn’t just walk to another counter, I accepted my fate and moved to the garage.

The most unsavory part about the Enterprise experience as it differs from other brands is the endless damage evaluation. Walking around with an iPad, the attendant points out a knick here, a scratch there – the perfect moment to take out the insurance or pay with a card that includes the Collision Damage Waiver just to avoid participation.

I can’t say for certain that the vehicle was used to move pounds of marijuana across state lines – I couldn’t say that at all. But I could say for certain that it smelled so deeply of weed that I doubt any amount of cleaning could be effective.

“This one smells like weed.” I said, shutting the door.

“I’ll have to take your word for it.” She replied and moved on.

Really? Would you have noticed if I said it smelled as though a den of skunks had made their home in the stow-and-go or would you have to take my word for it? I don’t want to show up to family smelling like backstage at Coachella.

We moved on to the vehicle next to it, a California tag with 51,000 miles and a quarter tank of gas. She started the walk around again, noting that the chip in the windshield could spider but I wouldn’t be responsible if the windshield needed to be replaced upon my return. Cool. How about not giving me a vehicle where I might have a spiderwebbed safety issue?

I tossed my luggage inside, and addressed her one more time.

I had to address the fuel level, as I might not make it to my first stop without the low fuel light illuminating.

“A quarter tank?” I was borderline ready to leave but knew that I didn’t have time to start this all over somewhere else.

“Those two guys in the wash bay sitting down on their phones – do they work here?”

“Yes.” She said it to me unironically without connecting the challenge of the cleanliness, or the useless fuel level and how both of those service challenges might have been solved (in the case of the skunky van, maybe not) by the staff being asked to do their jobs.

They aren’t understaffed, they are unbothered, indifferent, and at a minimum unwilling to ask them to perform their duties, or more likely, incapable of actual management. It’s a crazy position to take with Enterprise’s excellent corporate structure and the fact that they give you the tools to be your own boss.

I guess some things are just better in the movies.

In the words of our 43rd US President, “Fool me once, shame on – shame on you. Fool me – you can’t get fooled again.” It was simpler times when that sort of turn of phrase failure was the height of presidential gaffes.

I don’t care that National’s ownership is the same (ERAC), I will continue to rent from them as long as their model remains the same and continues to deliver. But from Enterprise? Never, ever again. Maybe a “neighborhood location” has different rules, but the staff at the Downtown Omaha location exhibited a total lack of interest in my experience or their own jobs. Corporate didn’t respond to my survey nor to my request for comment. And while I would agree that I’m not Cooper Anderson reaching out to them, readers in the past have asked if the brand has a comment. They did not.

I shouldn’t have to drive around in a dented safety concern reeking of weed while I get gas immediately after departing the parking lot and somehow try to perfectly return with a quarter tank or pay $7/gallon. It’s disrespectful to your clients but it appears the great corporate structure at Enterprise may have given this branch the tools to be their own boss, and they were even less interested in doing that than I am in renting from any Enterprise location anywhere.

Besides renting from them in the first place, my greatest regret was that I didn’t get to try my credit card’s Collision Damage Waiver on for size, just in case I needed it.

I have had terrible experiences with Enterprise in the past – being stranded with a disabled vehicle that could have been prevented by adequate maintenance, spurious cleaning charges, etc., I was forced to use Enterprise due to being at remote locations recently and was very pleased with their service. Sorry you were not as lucky.

I had a bad experience with Enterprise many years ago and stopped using them. A couple of years ago I booked with them when National was too expensive and had a good experience, and I have mostly booked with Enterprise ever since. All my recent experiences have been good. However, I have been booking almost exclusively at large or medium sized airports, so that could be the difference. They almost always have skip the counter and except at the largest airports they often share cars with National and Alamo anyway.

For best results, in an off airport location, try to use a car dealership. Perhaps one that has a relationship with friends or other local contacts. There you will find a few newer rentals in great condition that are not of skunk smell. These are not advertised but kept for the company. Cannot say they would honor t & c but at least you get a better choice.

You rented from Enterprise (at a non-airport) location. What could go wrong? Well, you learned what could go wrong.

From my experience, I’m not sure Enterprise is the problem. You wrote “maybe a neighborhood location has different rules” and I don’t think it’s different rules but perhaps different standards. And to be clear, this is the case for every rental car brand where I go to a neighborhood location – I used to do this often when I didn’t have a car, and I know that it is very different than the airport experience. Point by point… – Gas tank: more likely to be less than full, but that close to empty is particularly bad. In many neighborhood locations it is literally one person working the place. Still you need enough gas to drive it off the lot. – Cleanliness: Unacceptable. That sucks and reflects poorly on the brand. – Damage/Inspection: They always do the walkaround, and there’s almost always some damage they note. Many of mine had divots in the windshield or rear windshield and a couple door dings. Combined with there being one employee this process often means renting a car takes 20-30 minutes per person, which is another issue. – 24 hour rule: I don’t know of anywhere this is written but it is absolutely true at multiple brands that those booked within 24 hours are basically considered walk-ups in terms of availability. In fact there are usually printed signs when I go to the location saying as much. I rented from an Avis in a Portland suburb in the summer and multiple printed signs and a single unhappy employee greeted at least two people who had made reservations in the last day, showed up at 8am opening, and were turned away wholesale with no cars available on a random Thursday. I’m glad this story confirmed my assumption that it had to do with connection to real time inventory at corporate locations, as many neighborhood ones are franchises.

I do not disagree that this is a terrible experience, I’m just saying this is par for the course. I’ve rented at Enterprise, Hertz, and Avis neighborhood locations all with near-identical experiences, in San Diego, Portland, and San Francisco, for what it’s worth. Usually the neighborhood locations *inside* actual car dealerships (like a full-service Nissan dealer) are much better than the standalone or hotel-attached ones in the same city and have fewer of these problems, but they also tend to be open more limited hours.

Alex is right. Never use off-airport locations if you can avoid it. Most do not have good standards, and you are lucky if they have any decent car resembling the one you reserved available. If you have to, you might have slightly better luck at Hertz or Avis.

Sorry that you did have a bad experience with Enterprise I did have a very positive expriences (3) with them at a local office in Tysons corner

The car was clean, full tank, and all persons i dealt with were friendly and very efficient

“Thanks for the F shack – love Dirty Mike and the boys.”

Enterprise at least leaves you a jar of old mustard!

When I first started traveling regularly for work around 2012 and 2013, I used Enterprise. My first two employers had corporate contracts with the company.

I always had problems with Enterprise, mostly with branches taking reservations and then having no car available. Not just the particular car I had booked, but any car at all. It became such an issue that my second employer canceled its contract with Enterprise in 2014, the same year I left.

In late 2014 or early 2015, Delta and Hertz struck a deal that gave Delta Diamond medallions top-tier Hertz President’s Circle status. It worked great for a few years. Then Hertz went downhill during and afrter the pandemic and, in my opinion, has never recovered. I blindly stuck with Hertz for 10 years.

I will say with Hertz that it paid to get to know a manager at a branch you frequent. For example, around 2018, I was going to Honolulu for work once or twice a month. I did something like 18 trips in a 12-month period. I became “friends” with a supervisor or manager at the Honolulu airport branch. He always pre-blocked me into a Jeep Wrangler without me having to book one. That was great.

Then in 2020, I relocated for work on an 11.5-month contract. I arrived in early January. I made a booking for the whole year. Then the pandemic hit. Hertz wanted to sell my car. I’d get a new car every 3-4 weeks, when Hertz required me to come into the office for a vehicle inspection. They usually took the car and gave me something new. The manager always made sure they had something decent for me even though Hertz was selling virtually its entire fleet.

I tried Avis in 2024 and 2025. They matched me to their top tier, and, for whatever reason, I kept that status for a year and a half. President’s Club or Chairman’s Club. Something like that. I received a couple of decent upgrades without asking, but the service was awful.

Twice, an airport branch failed to close out my rental contract after I returned the car. Another branch refused to let me take a car because its system showed I still had an open rental at another location from more than a year earlier. It was a complete mess, and I could never get anyone at Avis to resolve it.

The final straw came when I prepaid for an Avis rental through the Delta Air Lines portal. The branch then charged me again, so I paid twice. Avis refused to issue a refund. I disputed the duplicate charge with Chase Visa, but Chase sided with Avis even though I supplied the documentation. I lost $700 and stopped renting from Avis.

In late 2025, I decided to give Enterprise another chance. Since then, I’ve rented from them about 25 times, totaling roughly 70 rental days in the United States, Canada, the UK, France, and Germany.

Customer service is generally very good at the branch level. Sometimes, employees are a little over the top in trying to please you. I’ve had locations knock $75 off the bill for relatively minor issues, even when I insisted no compensation was necessary.

The problem, just as in 2012 and 2013, is that many branches continue to accept bookings when they have no vehicles available. This happened to me at an Enterprise location in Zurich. Thankfully, Sixt had a car with an automatic transmission within my budget.

Enterprise also regularly gives me older vehicles or cars with higher mileage. I’ve paid for premium, vehicle-specific rentals, such as a Suburban or Jeep Wrangler, and received vehicles with 55,000 miles on them. Even the worst cars I rented from Hertz never had more than 20,000 or 25,000 miles on the odometer.

My other big issue with Enterprise is the lack of a choose-your-own-car aisle like Hertz offers. I have Enterprise Gold status, its second-highest tier, but I often have to wait in line to go through the charade with a staff member who then escorts me to the parking lot and finds me a car. I probably waste 10 to 15 minutes on this with every rental. I understand that Enterprise emphasizes personal interactions as part of its approach to customer service, but it’s just too much.

I also never get upgrades unless I ask. Ever. Sometimes I’ll ask and get a “sure, no problem,” but nothing is ever offered proactively.

The weed issue is more and more prevalent. I have had both Hertz and Avis vehicles in Louisiana given to me reeking of Snoop Dogg or Willie Nelson concerts and had to change. Recently they had no other cars so I was a stuck driving with windows down hoping to not be pulled over and lose my government clearance, because I am sure the local cops would buy the “it was already in the rental” story. I djd have the agent make a note before I left in ase something came up. I had an Uber once that reeked as I was going to an airport for an international flight (all I need is some drug to hit a d delay me at the border because of it). Just do it at home at home people!

#6294. The Best Blanket Scarves to Keep You Warm at 30,000 Feet

Anyone who has spent hours on a freezing airplane knows that a warm scarf can make all the difference. A blanket scarf is one of my favorite in-flight essentials: It's easy to throw on before boarding, doubles as an extra layer when cabin temperatures drop, and makes even the simplest airport outfit feel more put together. The best blanket scarves for travel balance comfort, versatility, and style. A large scarf can double as a shawl or blanket on long-haul flights, while lightweight cashmere scarves keep you warm without taking up too much room in your carry-on. Below, I've rounded up the best blanket scarves to travel with this season, from soft, oversized knits to packable, 100% cotton styles.

For those who prefer classic cashmere scarves, Aritzia's blanket scarf checks all the boxes. Made from 100% mid-weight cashmere, the soft jersey knit provides plenty of warmth without feeling too heavy. A narrow silhouette and rolled hem offer it a streamlined look. The cashmere is also verified to The Good Cashmere Standard, which promotes improved animal welfare practices.

The beauty of Eileen Fisher's Triangle scarf lies in how many ways you can wear it. Its triangular shape looks great draped over the shoulders, wrapped around the neck, or loosely tied for a more relaxed look. Made from fine Italian cashmere designed to grow softer over time, this versatile piece is one you'll reach for well beyond a single season.

There may be no brand more synonymous with cashmere than White + Warren, so it’s no surprise that its travel wrap is one of my favorites. I carried a navy version of it all over the country last winter, from a trip to The Green O in Montana down to Primland in Virginia. The light cashmere weave adds warmth without bulk, and its extra-long size means it can drape over my whole body during a plane nap.

Think of Free People's packable scarf as a miniature puffer jacket for your neck. Made from padded nylon, it's a cozy option for winter travel and outdoor adventures, whether you're checking into a cozy cabin or a ski resort. A concealed zip pocket keeps small essentials close, and the included pouch makes it easy to tuck into your carry-on or tote bag.

Long flights, chilly train rides, and overzealous air conditioning are no match for Zestt Organics' Dreamsoft travel scarf. Made from plush, 100% organic cotton, this large scarf measures 28x78" and doubles as a cozy shawl or travel blanket when you need extra coverage. It's also machine washable, making it an especially practical companion for trips near and far.

J.Crew's cashmere wrap, which comes in a range of colors from classic black to camel, is both cozy and sustainable. It's very oversized, keeping you fully covered on the plane, in the car, or even just on the couch. Even better, the company is the first US partner of Aid by Trade Foundation, a nonprofit that promotes sustainable agricultural development around the world.

Gap’s chic scarf combines cozy sherpa with edgy faux leather for an unexpected mix of textures. The rich, on-trend chocolate brown shade makes it especially appealing this season, perfect for city trips and holiday outings. Pair it with a wool coat or leather jacket, et voila.

Until Quince came along, it seemed that affordable cashmere was an oxymoron. But this direct-to-consumer brand has continually surprised me with the high quality of its products at prices that won’t make me cringe. Quince’s ribbed wrap is no exception: It’s a thick, sturdy weave that’s equally perfect around shoulders or as a lap blanket.

Sure, nothing is as soft as cashmere, but when it comes to keeping you toasty, no material beats a wool weave. Alo's wool scarf is very oversized; you can loop it around your neck several times or easily drape it on your shoulders during a chilly flight. Thanks to its extra-long length and thick material, it's a go-to for commerce editor Meaghan Kenny in the winter.

Who says scarves have to be strictly practical? Sofia Cashmere's wrap brings a little sparkle to cold-weather dressing with shimmering metallic fibers, delicate beading, and sequins. The soft, cashmere-blend knit drapes elegantly over the shoulders, adding a stylish finishing touch to fancier looks for holiday parties, evening outings, and winter weddings.

Material: Cashmere, metallic fibers, nylon

Jacquemus' Carro scarf is anything but subtle. Measuring nearly eight-and-a-half feet long, this oversized scarf takes winter accessorizing to the next level. The fuzzy, mohair-alpaca blend adds texture, and there's also an embroidered grosgrain logo. Wrap it around your neck a few times or let the extra-long ends hang loose for maximum impact.

As the name implies, this wrap is a generous piece of fabric that’s 44" wide by 72" long. The material is a sleek mix of 95% Tencel modal and 5% spandex; the stretch is key for allowing it to drape just so. I love that it comes in a handful of seasonal colors, from a deep plum you can even wear to a fancy dinner, to a muted sand that would pair well with anything in your suitcase. Plus, it’s fully machine washable and can go in the dryer without shrinking.

A blanket scarf is a large, oversized wrap that offers more coverage than a traditional scarf. Typically made from cozy materials like wool, cashmere, or cotton, you can wrap it around your neck, drape it over your shoulders, or wear it as a shawl. Some are even large enough to double as a blanket.

Blanket scarves are especially useful for air travel because they can serve as both a stylish accessory and an extra layer when cabin temperatures drop. Look for soft, breathable fabrics like cotton or cashmere that feel comfortable against your skin.

What are the most packable blanket scarves?

The most packable blanket scarves are typically made from lightweight, flexible fabrics that fold down easily without taking up too much suitcase space. Cashmere scarves are a great option because they provide warmth without excessive bulk. For something specifically designed for travel, Free People's Pixie Packable Puffer scarf folds into an included pouch, while Zestt Organics' Dreamsoft travel scarf offers the versatility of a scarf, shawl, and blanket all in one.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless stands out in the Marriott card suite thanks to its solid lineup of perks, including an annual free night award (certain hotels have resort fees) and elite night credits, for a relatively low annual fee.

Whether you are a frequent Marriott guest or want a few extra perks the next time you stay with the brand, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless makes sense for a wide range of travelers. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

The is a cobranded card between Marriott Bonvoy and Chase. The card earns Marriott Bonvoy points, which can be used to book free nights at more than 10,000 properties worldwide.

The best way to redeem Marriott points is for free nights at Marriott hotels and resorts. However, you can also transfer your points to airline partners.

Marriott Bonvoy Boundless provides a standout suite of perks, including an annual free night award and automatic Silver Elite status, for a $95 annual fee.

I find it especially impressive that a mid-tier hotel card with a modest annual fee offers such lucrative perks, especially the annual free night award. Certain hotels have resort fees.

Here's a breakdown of the perks included with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless:

You don't have to go all in on Marriott to get a lot out of having this $95-annual-fee card in your wallet, and that's what makes the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless worth considering.

Related: Marriott Bonvoy elite status 'soft landing' policy: How to requalify for status

The packs a punch for its reasonable annual fee. Here's what cardholders can expect.

Given TPG's November 2026 valuation of Marriott points at 0.75 cents apiece, the 35,000-point certificate is worth $263. This is nearly three times the card's $95 annual fee and is a fantastic benefit, especially since you don't have to spend on the card to earn the certificate.

While the Silver Elite status on the card is the first of Marriott's elite status tiers, it does offer a few useful benefits, such as a 10% points bonus on paid stays and priority late checkout.

If you put at least $35,000 of spending on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless in a calendar year, you'll earn Gold Elite status. This comes with more perks, such as a 25% points boost and enhanced room upgrade (when available).

For most cardholders, it’s hard to justify putting $35,000 in purchases on the card solely to earn Gold Elite status.

If Gold Elite status is your goal, you may be better off combining the card's 15 complimentary elite night credits with 10 paid nights; this totals 25 elite nights needed for Gold Elite status.

If you're eligible for a business card, you can also pair the 15 elite night credits given by the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless with 15 elite night credits provided by the . These 30 total elite night credits leave you with just 20 nights to earn Platinum Elite.

You can also reach a higher elite status by earning one elite night credit for every $5,000 spent on purchases with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless.

Related: How to choose a no-foreign-transaction-fee credit card

Given TPG's relatively low valuation of Marriott points, I only recommend paying for Marriott stays with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless. There are other cards on the market that earn more valuable rewards on dining, gas and groceries.

The best way to redeem your Marriott points is to book free nights at one of the brand's hotels.

Since Marriott uses dynamic award pricing (meaning the number of points needed fluctuates based on demand and availability), you may have to take extra time and effort to strategize for maximum value.

Marriott has an award calendar search function that can help narrow down the best deal for your points. For example, a night at the Moxy NYC Lower East Side in January 2027 could cost as few as 57,000 points per night or as many as 81,000 points per night, depending on when you book.

While we value Marriott points at 0.75 cents apiece, there are ways to get better value.

For instance, TPG lead writer for loyalty programs Katie Genter previously redeemed 112,000 points for a five-night stay at the Courtyard by Marriott Toronto Vaughan for a music festival. Compared against a cash rate of $1,464, she got an impressive 1.31 cents per point from this redemption.

Also, keep in mind that Marriott offers a fifth-night-free benefit. When you book at least five consecutive nights on points, you'll get the night that's worth the lowest number of points for free. This can help you stretch your points for longer trips.

Marriott points are also transferable to nearly 40 airline partners, most at a 3:1 ratio. These include some hard-to-earn currencies, such as Air China PhoenixMiles and Frontier Airlines.

However, unless you have a specific airline redemption in mind and need to top off your balance, transferring is unlikely to be the best use of your points.

The current offer delivers decent value for new cardholders. That said, we've seen stronger welcome offers on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless in the past.

I find the to be an excellent choice for a wide range of travelers, from Marriott loyalists who don't want to pay a high annual fee to those who occasionally stay at the brand's hotels and resorts.

Of course, if you're a fierce Marriott loyalist chasing status, a more premium card may be a better choice. And, if you want an option that earns higher-value rewards at a better rate on everyday purchases, you may want to look at a general travel card that earns transferable rewards.

Overall, however, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless certainly provides enough ongoing value in exchange for its modest $95 annual fee, making it worth keeping year after year.

#6292. We Keep Going Back To Germany. This Family Trip Reminded Me Why.

We landed in Zürich on SAS and drove to my in-law’s home in Southwest Germany, about an hour away.

There are border checks now as you enter Germany from France and Switzerland, though usually (I’m just saying…) when they see it’s white people they just waive you through.

And I’ll leave off the politics here (because I’d rather focus on getting our own house in order in the USA), but I think this picture says it all about Germany these days:

We tend to stop at DM (a drug store chain) at the start of each trip because it’s on the way home and we always come with a list since so many products here are cheaper and better than their American counterparts, even with the stronger Euro. One thing I like about DM (well, liked…) was that they had a free water dispenser with cups.

In Germany water is an annoyance when going out…most restaurants and coffee shops frown on tap water (unlike in France and the Netherlands), so you’re paying everywhere €5-8EUR for bottles you can buy for 50-80 Euro cents in the grocery store. It’s nice to “hydrate” at DM, but for TWO YEARS the water machine has been broken.

How in the heck can you not fix this for two years (unless, as I suppose, the point is that you don’t want to offer free water any longer)?!

It was a bit warm for the time of the year, but not unpleasant. How nice it was to be back and over the next several days we enjoyed a lot of quality time together, with good döner, coffee, and ice cream.

There was a fairly intense lighting storm that was just beautiful to sit out on the patio and watch:

One morning I decided to ride by myself to Basel for coffee…there was a new place I wanted to try called Mantila Coffee…it was SO GOOD (my new favorite coffee spot in Basel) and I had such a nice chat with the owner. I’m going to update my Basel Coffee post with a couple of places I tried on this trip.

Augustine was livid that biked to Basel without him, so we returned the next day (sadly Mantila is closed on Saturday), but we found another great place called Tinka. Augustine wanted his own coffee…I had a cortado, he had cappuccino, and then we split a delicious sparkling blood orange drink.

My father-in-law likes a restaurant called Gasthaus Krone in the hamlet of Lehnacker, located really right in the middle of the Schwarzwald (Black Forest). The food is delicious indeed.

One cool part of this trip is that my daughter finally got the hang of riding her bike herself…we just don’t feel it’s safe to ride bikes at home (due to fast drivers…see here for a laugh) but it was fun to see her so excited.

To celebrate, we had (more) ice cream together.

Join our mailing list for a daily summary of posts! We never sell your info.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Time in the city and time in the country. Travel and family. Time spent in community (faith based or otherwise). Coffee. All are non-optional for a well lived life. Hope you enjoyed the trip.

Enjoy Augustine being livid at being left out. Assuming he is emotionally healthy, you have only a few years before he concludes you are a square he wants to avoid.

4 Swiss Francs for an espresso that costs 1 Euro in Italy. Oh well…….

I really enjoy visiting Germany. Unfortunately my language skills are near zero.

And yeah, the politics/issues in Germany are also not good at times. I have an Italian friend who lives north of Munich and was telling us of issues. Her son is finishing up college/school there and actually has 4 different passports.

Most of our trips have been the typical shorter tourist trips but I would like a multi-week trip to explore the countryside.

Keep taking the trips, even if the kids miss a bit of school. As the child of parents that placed high value on family, travel and experiences, I learned far more visiting family in Germany and traveling Europe than I did sitting in the classroom.

Very nice. Thanks for sharing the slice of life with us.

#6291. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6290. 10 Spacious Villas in Morocco Fit for a Relaxing Group Getaway

The bustling capital city has perennial charm, but beyond its walls, there’s so much more to Morocco worth exploring. Whether you’re gearing up for a hiking trip to the Atlas mountains, looking to immerse yourself in the sights and sounds of the buzzy souks or headed out to the coast, there’s a fantastic nearby address to know. Most of our favorite Morocco villas pair idyllic views with in-house chefs, housekeepers, and even security staff for a hotel-worthy break in your own space. Below are 10 of the best villas in Morocco to rent for your next trip.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost or Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Bed & bath: 5 bedrooms, 5 bathroomsTop amenities: Heated pool, home cinema, sauna and steam room

This is the kind of holiday home that keeps everyone happy, making it perfect for a large family with different ideas of what a great holiday looks like. The interiors are modern, but Moroccan charm is preserved in the details. The five spacious bedrooms all feature en suite bathrooms and are spread across both floors. The large living area, with its circular arrangement of comfortable sofas, and the home cinema invite guests to relax and enjoy each other's company during their stay. A fitness center and a traditional hammam add a wellness touch to the home. There is a golf course right next door, should you fancy a round of golf.

Bed & bath: 8 bedrooms, 7 bathroomsTop amenities: Pool, hammam, pickleball court, pétanque, barbecue

Located just north of Marrakech, this villa gives groups a soft, quiet place to land after a busy day in the city—and plenty of activities to keep everyone busy on days spent on-site. Beyond the resort-style heated swimming pool lined with lounge chairs, the pétanque and pickleball courts encourage some healthy competition. Afterwards, spend a bit of relaxation time in the hammam or massage room, or kick back in the garden. Of note, two of the eight bedrooms are located in an annex of the villa and share a bathroom.

Bed & bath: 6 bedrooms, 6 bathroomsTop amenities: Heated pool, outdoor dining space

To reach this villa, you have to drive 30 minutes from Marrakech into the stunning Ourika Valley. On arrival, you’ll immediately notice the snow-capped peaks of the Atlas Mountains rising around the property. The 8,000-square-meter garden dotted with olive trees and cacti is the perfect setting for days spent lying by the large pool, playing pétanque, or cooking up a storm with produce from the organic kitchen garden. Inside, the house is bathed in sunlight and particularly stunning at dawn. There are six bedrooms, all featuring en suite bathrooms for ultimate comfort. Five of the bedrooms are in the main house—as well as the kitchen and the spacious living room featuring a dining space with a fireplace—while the final bedroom is in the annex, alongside the playroom and wellness area with a hammam.

Bed & bath: 6 bedrooms, 6 bathsTop amenities: Terrace, pool, hot tub, gym

Bed & bath: 6 bedrooms, 7 bathsTop amenities: Pool, terraces, Atlas Mountains views

Palais Les Orchidées is a palace-like six-suite villa just outside the center of Marrakech, combining grand architecture with pared-back interiors and views towards the Atlas Mountains. The property is surrounded by leafy gardens, with a large swimming pool and several terraces providing plenty of space to relax outdoors. Inside, all six suites have king-size beds and en suite bathrooms with bathtubs and showers, making this a particularly comfortable option for a large group or several couples traveling together. Despite its peaceful setting, you won’t be too far from the action: the villa is around 15 minutes by car from some of Marrakech’s best-known sights, including the Koutoubia, Bahia Palace, and Jardin Majorelle, and around 20 minutes from Marrakech Menara Airport. Breakfast can also be served at the villa for an additional charge.

Bed & bath: 5 bedrooms, 5 bathsTop amenities: Rooftop terrace, private pool, breakfast chef

This classic Marrakech riad is a bohemian dream with vibrant, patterned tiles, a mishmash of colorful, soft furnishings, and a beautiful outdoor courtyard—bringing good vibes only. You’ll be well taken care of here; daily housekeeping, a breakfast chef, and a night guard will ensure everything goes swimmingly. Take an alfresco lunch before a dip in the plunge pool, then settle on the daybed for a leisurely afternoon with a view—there’s a panoramic vista of both the buzzing medina and the Atlas mountain range. Take note: You’ll have to climb some steps to reach this villa, and there’s no parking outside, so if you’re taking a car, you’ll need to leave it a short distance away. However, there are a slew of excellent restaurants and hammams within walking distance and good public transport links right outside.

Bed & bath: 9 bedrooms, 9 bathsTop amenities: Outdoor kitchen, sauna/steam room, gym

Like most experiences in Morocco, stepping into this palatial villa’s vast grounds is a sensory feast from the get-go. Plaster pink walls, an eclectic mix of bright furniture, ornate artwork, patterned rugs, and glittering chandeliers are wrapped around the central turquoise jewel of the outdoor pool. It has nine huge bedrooms, at least one of which has a statement roll-top tub in the corner, plus nine bathrooms—so no waiting in line for the shower here. It’s a great choice for bachelor or bachelorette parties and big group getaways, with multiple comfy gathering spaces for catch-ups with a view. First, head to the meeting room to grab a drink from the bar, but take them to the rooftop terrace to maximize the experience—the views at sunset are fantastic. Extra bookable spa and hammam treatments make a stay in this Moroccan palace all the sweeter.

Bed & bath: 8 bedrooms, 8 bathsTop amenities: Private pool, courtyard, outdoor shower, record player

This isn’t a riad, but a former fondouk—a 19th-century inn that used to accommodate travelers before they set sail on trading voyages. Now, however, it has been transformed into a chic villa for 15, set around four distinct courtyard spaces decorated with fragrant lemon trees and mature prickly cacti. Locally sourced clay walls bring traditional flair that keeps you cool on hot Moroccan nights, and there’s a pool to jump into for welcome midday dips. Active types, take note. This villa sits in the ancient walled city of Taraudant, which offers easy access to both the High Access and Anti-Atlas hiking routes. It's the perfect place to wind down after a long day of mountain treks.

Bed & bath: 4 bedrooms, 4 bathsTop amenities: Terrace, courtyard, fireplace, private cook

Bed & bath: 2 bedrooms, 3 bathsTop amenities: Private chefs, private heated pool, terrace

With a hilltop location looking down onto sparkling sea views, even by Moroccan standards, the views here are unbeatable. A clever design means the home provides ample opportunity to totally immerse yourself in the landscape. Run a bath in the outdoor tub right on the beachfront, and awake to sunrise light streaming through floor-to-ceiling windows framing gentle ocean waves. Mealtimes are sorted thanks to the in-house private chefs who’ll cook up anything you please to be enjoyed alfresco with a glass of wine on the terrace next to the private heated pool. There’s a slew of activities on offer in Essaouira—tell the hosts what you’d like to do and they’ll make it happen.

#6289. Teamsters Sue Horizon Air Over Pilot Rest Rules

The Teamsters have sued Horizon Air, alleging the Alaska Air Group subsidiary violated federal labor law by changing how it handles pilots who report fatigue.

The Teamsters Airline Division and Local 1224 filed the lawsuit Oct. 23 in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. The union alleges Horizon requires pilots who report fatigue at their home base to travel to another city as passengers before taking the rest provided under their contract.

The union alleges the practice violates the Railway Labor Act and is asking the court to order Horizon to stop it and restore the negotiated rest protections.

“Management cannot pick and choose which parts of our contract it wants to follow,” said Sean Lenney, a Horizon pilot and member of Local 1224, in a news release.

The Teamsters also said Thursday that 99% of pilots who voted backed a no-confidence measure against Carlos Zendejas, Horizon’s senior vice president of operations. The union’s Horizon Air Pilots Executive Council called for his removal following the vote.

Horizon and its pilots have been negotiating a new collective bargaining agreement for more than three and a half years, according to the union. Pilots held informational pickets in Seattle and Boise, Idaho, on Oct. 15 over issues including pay, staffing, and training.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

Earlier this year, I was in the middle of a United Airlines status challenge, and I saw an offer for a new credit card with a nice welcome offer that I couldn't resist. I hadn't really played too deeply in the United ecosystem and didn't have any of Chase's United-branded credit cards.

Interestingly, I had a United Airlines debit card in the early 2000's, but that was closed on me when the U.S. passed the Durbin Amendment as part of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act of 2010.

That locked many of us out of lucrative points earning on debit cards.

Anyway, I was excited when I was able to open the (see rates and fees).

Of course, I quickly earned the generous 90,000-mile and 3,000 PQP welcome bonus after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening and adding an authorized user (no longer available), but I was just as excited to learn I had many perks that came with the card, which I've continued to enjoy this year.

Currently, new cardholders can earn up to 90,000 bonus miles and 500 PQPs: earn 500 PQPs after your first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Here is what comes with the card, which pleasantly surprised me after I got it.

One thing I didn't realize when I signed up for the card was that cardholders get a $200 United travel credit. That came in handy when I needed to book a recent flight to Montana to see my father.

I used the card's $200 annual United TravelBank cash to offset the $488 round-trip ticket cost for my flight from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Bozeman International Airport (BZN). So that trip cost me just $288. Score.

While I haven't used it yet, this card includes up to $150 in hotel credits each year at Renowned Hotels and Resorts for United® Cardmembers. I'm going to try to get a stay in this year to earn that valuable credit.

Here's a potential option that Chase has listed in Bozeman. I stayed at the Kimpton Armory Hotel Bozeman by IHG when it first opened, and it would be a fun hotel to return to this year.

The Quest card also comes with an up to $150 JSX flight credit each anniversary year, up to $180 in Instacart credits each calendar year (through Dec. 31, 2027), and up to $80 ($40 each) in rental car credits each anniversary year for your first and second Avis or Budget rental when you book through cars.united.com. I haven't used any of those perks yet.

I have used the ride-hailing statement credits a few times. You get up to $100 in ride-hailing statement credits with this card (up to $8 monthly from January through November and up to $12 in December; yearly activation required). So far this year, I've used it five times, saving $40.

Finally, there's also a $120 Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or Nexus credit every four years.

Related: United card bonuses: Best-ever offers on 2 of the personal cards

The Quest card comes with some pretty good mileage multipliers. You get 10 total miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights and 4 miles per dollar spent on other eligible United purchases (like onboard food). You also get 2 miles per dollar spent on dining, select streaming services and all other travel.

Note that your mileage earning on Basic Economy and base option tickets may differ from the Quest's standard 10 total miles per dollar spent rate.

I found the miles really added up when I was going for the minimum spend to earn my welcome bonus.

The card also comes with 1,000 bonus Premier qualifying points (PQPs) each year that can give you a head start on earning United elite status. While I was completing my minimum spend, I ended up qualifying for United Silver status, which comes with things like extra-legroom seats starting 24 hours before your flight.

I earned 3,000 PQPs when I opened the card (The current welcome offer includes 500 PQPs after your first purchase). That gave me a huge push toward the 6,000 PQPs I needed for Silver status.

I was able to use my Silver status on that same trip to Montana when I picked Economy Plus seats at check-in.

My Silver status also gives me the possibility for complimentary upgrades, available 24 hours before departure (though they are very few and far between for Silver-level elite status holders).

One of the most incredible perks of holding the Quest card is that it gives you access to additional Saver-level award availability and a discount of at least 10% on award flights.

I was able to spend just 85,000 miles for a one-way flight from Tokyo to Chicago and then on to Newark. That flight could have cost someone without status and the Quest card as much as 450,000 United miles.

In fact, United says my card has saved me 165,000 miles this year alone already.

The Quest card also gets you priority boarding in Group 2, which can mean the difference between being able to bring your carry-on bags onboard or having to gate check them. It also comes with two free checked bags and an annual 10,000-mile award flight discount starting on your first card anniversary.

While I don't love the $350 annual fee on the card, it's partially offset by the generous $200 United travel credit I receive each year. The annual 10,000-mile discount to use toward an eligible award flight is also worth at least $200 to me with my award booking patterns. Together, these two perks alone offset the card's annual fee.

I was mostly interested in the generous welcome bonus when I opened the United Quest Card, but I've been pleasantly surprised by how much additional value I've gotten from it. From the $200 United travel credit to the elite-status boost and the huge savings on award flights, the card has easily earned back the $350 annual fee for me in value.

The Quest card has turned out to be a real winner and will keep a place in my wallet going forward.

#6287. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6286. American Airlines Makes Hotel Vouchers Easier To Get, But Warns Of Fewer Hotel Choices

American Airlines is updating how it provides hotel rooms, food credits, and transportation to passengers stranded by flight disruptions. Getting help without standing in another long line is welcome. But an internal memo also warns that employees may have fewer hotel choices to offer, which leaves me wondering whether a faster voucher will necessarily mean a better night.

View From The Wing highlights a November employee memo outlining changes to American’s Hotel, Meal and Transportation system, known internally as HMT.

American was already promoting automatic disruption vouchers in 2025. The question now is whether the latest changes make that assistance more reliable and easier to use.

I recently wrote about my American Airlines flight from Chicago to Los Angeles that nearly became an overnight stay.

A 7:10 p.m. departure slipped repeatedly until the posted departure time reached 11:55 p.m. The aircraft was there, but we had no pilots. Eventually, pilots arrived from Dallas and received a chorus of cheers from passengers who were thrilled we might actually get home.

During the wait, an Admirals Club agent offered me a hotel room if I wanted to rebook for the next day. The offer came with a caveat:

I appreciated having an option, but I wanted to get to Los Angeles. By that point, an airport hotel would have meant a short night followed by another trip through security and another flight.

But it is a reason why I appreciate this new rollout. Every minute spent waiting for an agent to arrange accommodation is a minute you cannot spend sleeping. If American can deliver a usable hotel offer to your phone promptly, that is a practical improvement.

“Frontline teams may see fewer hotel choices displayed than they are accustomed to seeing.”

Yes, a shorter list of suitable properties could work perfectly well and it is too early to say whether the remaining hotel options will be worse. But I’m not all that optimistic, here.

What happens when the available hotel is far from the airport, has no functioning shuttle at that hour, or cannot accommodate a family in an appropriate room.

We are not talking about putting every stranded passenger in a luxury hotel. But I do expect a clean room and a workable way to get there and back. A voucher is useful only if the accommodation behind it is suitable.

My agent’s Hilton comment was amusing, but it also captured the uncertainty. When you accept an airline-arranged room late at night, you may have little idea what you are getting.

Uber Central allows businesses to request rides for customers who do not have the Uber app. Riders receive trip details and a tracking link by text.

That could be particularly helpful for someone who rarely uses rideshare services or is already overwhelmed by a disrupted journey.

According to the reported instructions, however, hotel shuttles remain the first option, followed by Uber vouchers. Agent-arranged rides are intended for exceptions when those options do not meet the passenger’s needs. Broad availability of the new arrangement has not yet been established.

I hope agents have enough discretion to solve the actual problem. A hotel shuttle listed in a database is no help if it stopped running an hour ago…as a practical aside, before you leave the airport terminal call the hotel to make sure that the shuttle is running.

Under American’s published customer service plan, when a disruption is caused by the airline, assistance available upon request includes:

The plan also promises reimbursement of reasonable hotel costs if American cannot provide an approved hotel voucher (with an almost impossible caveat that such authorization must be obtained in writing). For disruptions beyond its control, such as weather, American generally leaves passengers responsible for their own accommodation and meals.

If you qualify for assistance and no automatic offer arrives, ask an agent. And if you get the food/beverage voucher, realize that the $12 won’t go very far (unless you are in Denver).

American Airlines deserves credit for making disruption assistance easier to deliver. Passengers who have already lost hours to a delay should not have to lose another hour obtaining a hotel voucher.

But fewer hotel choices could limit the usefulness of that improvement. I will judge the system by whether it gets stranded passengers into suitable rooms promptly, with transportation that actually works.

On my recent Chicago flight, I was thankful the pilots arrived and I never needed the hotel. Next time, I may not be so fortunate…(or maybe next time I will fly Delta or United).

#6285. How to Spend a Rainy Day in New York City

A rainy day in New York City is no new phenomenon, but that doesn’t make its occurrence any less disappointing. According to reporting from News 12, Central Park only reported nine completely dry weekends out of the past 40 weekends of 2026, putting a real—forgive me—damper on park hangs and beach days. In case you count yourself among the masses with foiled plans, we at Condé Nast Traveler have you covered. Our editors have weathered their fair share of cold and dreary days in the city and learned to love the rain. After all, it’s the best excuse to dry off by the crackling fireplace of a plush hotel lobby, or conversely, to take a dip into the steaming Russian Turkish baths to cure the sinking cold. Instead of willing the clouds to part, bear your galoshes and head to our editors’ favorite things to do in New York City on a rainy day.

That travel editors love a hotel lobby is about as unsurprising as a dad joke, but there’s nothing like a mini staycation to salvage a lost weekend. Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is partial to The Hotel Chelsea. The neighborhood institution has moved far past its roach-ridden days when Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe were Just Kids, and the experience of their lobby is the apotheosis of that evolution. There’s a lot of modern polish, sure, but all the charming verdigris has been kept intact. There’s the art from the hotel’s most (in)famous guests splashed over the walls, the wrought iron chandeliers bathing the space in romantic lighting, and the aforementioned fireplace tying a bow around the mood. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that the hotel’s Lobby Bar is just right next door. If Chelsea feels like a slog to commute to, there are plenty of great options scattered across the map, from the Ace Hotel Brooklyn which has plenty of public workspaces, or Times Square’s Algonquin Hotel, which saw the genesis of The New Yorker just 100 years ago.

The easiest remedy for rainy day restlessness is to stretch your legs at one of the city’s finest museums, though even the impressive 2.2 million-square-foot expanse of the Met becomes easily dwarfed when you’re crammed in by a surge of fellow museum-goers who had the exact same idea. Instead, spend your day exploring NYC’s smaller scholarly corners. Editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez heads to East Williamsburg art organization Amant whenever she feels like she’s cooped inside her apartment, watching the hours just slip away. To start, there’s no need to worry about ponying up big ticket prices as entry is always free. “Peruse the titles at Kis Café and Bookstore, then head to gallery spaces 932 Grand and 315 Maujer; across the street, you’ll find multimedia installations in Géza,” says Alvarez, “The exhibit Sentient Earth currently spans all three galleries, bringing together 28 artists to examine the ways we’ve impacted the planet (and what—if it gained sentience—its response to us might be). Do explore Amant's event programming of screenings and panels, which you can find here.” Other small but mighty options include the Financial District’s public poetry library Poets House, which overlooks the Hudson and Bushwick’s Bone Museum, which also houses resident tuxedo cat Bone Jovi.

Film critic Anthony Lane once posited, “as a rough rule, cinema can be sundered into two halves: six-o’clock films and nine-o’clock films,” and a rainy day is certainly the occasion for the six-o’clock variety and all its ritual: rallying a group to go with, booking the early dinner reservation, whiling away at a nearby bar after to unpack what you’ve just seen. Commerce director Madison Flager likes the Lincoln Center AMC, home to the largest IMAX screen in the country, clocking in at 75.6 feet tall by 101 feet wide, which is roughly the size of a 10-story building. News editor Hannah Towey, on the other hand, dodges the rain at the Metrograph, a boutique two-screen theater keeping the spirit of Prohibition-era New York alive and well. Whichever way you lean, you can always count on NYC’s trusty movie theaters to show you something new.

The less-than-stellar weather shouldn’t keep you from embarking on a treasure hunt, and doing your due diligence enclosed inside one of the city’s coolest vintage stores is a surefire way to uncover a few gems. Alvarez recommends the Flatiron District’s Surrender Dorothy, where the racks are piled with the well-loved and pristine, collector’s items and forgotten blasts from the past, avant-garde art pieces, and buy-it-for-life workwear. It’s dopamine dressing at its best. You could also try your luck at one of the city’s larger franchises like Beacon’s Closet, or, if you’re willing to face the elements, dive into a flea market.

One of the best spots to people-watch in the city, come rain or shine, is the baths. And having a place to hide from the chill and unforgiving precipitation is a welcome bonus. Commerce writer Jessica Sulima touts the East Village’s Russian Turkish Baths as the perfect place to drop by. Melt away whatever’s ailing you in the 215 °F Russian Sauna, and if you need any help doing so, get the platza oak leaf ritual where spa employees forcefully smack your pores open with bushels of oak leaves in the sauna. If you’re looking for something a little more communal, Flager likes to warm up at Othership, which sets itself apart with its guided wellness experiences that combine breath work, aromatherapy, visualizations, somatic movement, live music, and group “shares.”

Nothing brings a bar together like its pool table, but if you’ve spent more time watching the queue of quarters waiting for your turn than the game itself, head to a dedicated pool hall instead, where there’s a better chance of scoring a table all your own and watching the real pros practice their hand. Union Square’s Amsterdam Billiards has been a staple ever since I came to the city five years ago. The 11,000-square-foot hall decked with its array of Brunswick tables might seem intimidating at first, but take it from a real amateur: they may be serious about their snooker here, but they’re not snobby. Pool aside, patrons keep occupied with the hall’s other offerings like table tennis, beer pong, and darts. If you’re serious about upping your game, you can even book one-hour lessons with their in-house pros.

Jazz is one of the country’s greatest art forms, and New York is the genre’s most inspiring muse and resourceful studio. The city cemented its status in the 1920s Harlem Renaissance when legendary venues like the Cotton Club and Small’s Paradise put Duke Ellington, Fats Waller, and Billie Holiday in the national consciousness. Jazz in the city has traveled beyond its uptown crucible, and there’s great clubs peppered throughout the boroughs. Some of our favorites include Ornithology Jazz Club, which also has a killer vegan menu; Funny Bar, which comes from the same team as Baby’s All Right; and Greenwich Village’s Smalls Jazz Club, which keeps things true to form and no-frills.

New York’s historic theatre scene is far from confined to Broadway’s flashing lights. Some of the most exciting, intimate, and interactive productions in the city are playing Off-Broadway. Big names like Andrew Lloyd Webber have found a second wind in shows like Masquerade, a roving retelling of Phantom of the Opera, and fresh concepts like Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody are attracting their own audiences with their lower budget, DIY charm. Shows like these are a trove of talent, and odds are you can find one where you won’t have to pay an arm and a leg for entry at venues like La MaMa or Signature Theatre.

Associate social media manager Bridget Knowles swears by the people's princess of a dive bar as a haven from the harsh weather: “Interjecting here with what I’m sure we’re all thinking. I mean, sheesh. This is unspoken. A great dive bar is an oasis in New York City on a rainy day: a grunge mecca, a throw-some-hours-away swan song. My kind of place. A healthy dose of grime on an already lyrically imposing, moody day is great for the soul. Even if you’re off the Miller High Life (ah, it hurt to type, but pun intended) one of the greatest pastimes in life, according to me, is to simply load up touch tunes and shoot at a table a bit. Make some friends, watch something insane playing on a corner TV. You know, commiserate. Get your hands on some of the best in the city here.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6284. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6283. Southwest Airlines Offers “Free” Same-Day Flight Changes, But There’s A Seat-Fee Trap

Southwest Airlines offers eligible passengers free same-day flight changes, but there is a catch if you paid separately for your seat. Asking an airport agent to make the change can leave that seat purchase nonrefundable, while making the change through the app, website, or telephone receives different treatment. Apparently, how you change your flight now matters almost as much as which flight you choose.

View From The Wing highlights a peculiar provision in Southwest’s seat refund and exchange policy.

For passengers who separately purchased a seat on their original flight, Southwest explicitly states:

“Same-day change requested at the airport: Seat purchased on original flight is non-refundable.”

But complete that same-day change through Southwest.com, the Southwest app, or by telephone, and the rules provide a way to apply the original seat payment toward a replacement or receive a refund when buying a more expensive seat.

You could be standing at the gate with your phone in hand, looking at an earlier departure. Whether you tap the screen or ask the employee in front of you for help could affect what happens to money you already spent.

The policy concerns seats purchased separately from the airfare. Here is how Southwest describes the treatment when you voluntarily switch flights:

For a hypothetical example, suppose you paid $40 for a seat and make a confirmed same-day change through the app. If the replacement seat costs $30, Southwest applies the original payment but does not return the $10 difference.

If the replacement costs $50, you pay $50 upfront and generally receive a separate $40 refund. You should therefore check that the refund actually arrives rather than assuming the system simply charged you the difference.

Under Southwest’s same-day change policy, the confirmed-change benefit is available with Choice, Choice Preferred, and Choice Extra fares, along with Getaways by Southwest vacation bookings.

You need an available seat on a flight between the same origin and destination airports on the same travel date. The change must occur at least 10 minutes before your original scheduled departure.

Basic passengers must upgrade to an eligible fare first (and A-List or A-List Preferred status alone does not make a Basic ticket eligible for a free confirmed same-day change)

So when it comes to standby, there are two separate things to check: whether you can switch flights without an additional airfare charge, and what happens to the seat you purchased.

Do not confuse a confirmed change with same-day standby.

A confirmed change secures your place on the replacement flight immediately. Standby means waiting for space to become available, often much closer to boarding or even after boarding commences if you are waiting for no-shows. Southwest’s seat policy says the original seat purchase becomes nonrefundable when standby clears, regardless of how you joined the list.

Using the app therefore does not solve the seat-payment issue for standby. The eligibility rules differ too. A-List and A-List Preferred members can qualify for standby on Basic fares, even though those fares do not qualify for free confirmed same-day changes.

Of course, switching flights does not guarantee the same seat. Someone who bought extra legroom on one departure cannot reasonably expect an identical seat to materialize on a replacement flight. But why should the channel used to request the change determine the treatment of the original payment?

If Southwest can apply or refund that purchase when I use its app, why should asking an airport employee produce a less favorable rule? There may be a systems explanation, but that does little for a passenger who reasonably assumes an agent can provide the same options available online. On the other hand, I would bet that an agent who assigns you a superior seat in these sorts of situations is not going to charge for it…any frequent Southwest travelers want to weigh in?

This also puts employees in an awkward position. A passenger asks for help, receives it, then discovers that handling the transaction another way could have preserved the value of a seat purchase. For an airline that built so much goodwill around simplicity, this seems like an unnecessarily complicated way to handle a relatively ordinary request.

If you paid separately for a Southwest seat and want to make a confirmed same-day flight change, check the app or website before asking an airport agent to process it. Telephone changes also receive the more favorable treatment outlined in the policy.

Compare the replacement seat cost and keep track of any refund due. If you are using standby, remember that the app does not preserve the refundability of your original seat purchase once you clear.

A free flight change can still have consequences for the extras you purchased. Southwest passengers now have another reason to read the fine print before accepting what sounds like a straightforward benefit.
