#6267. Buy IHG One Rewards Points With 100% Bonus (0.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Through 11:59PM ET on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is tiered, as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status.

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses. With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 200,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 400,000 points at a cost of $2,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 200,000 points, pre-bonus.

When IHG One Rewards does offer a promotion on purchased points, the 100% bonus or 50% discount is the most common offer. A 100% bonus and 50% discount give you the same price per point, so you’ll typically pay 0.5 cents per point during a promotion.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through November 10, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

Do you plan on buying IHG points with a bonus?

#6266. Southwest 737 Flew 44 Times Before Wind Damage Was Found

A Southwest Boeing 737 MAX 8 flew 44 times before maintenance crews discovered tail damage that investigators traced to a thunderstorm more than a week earlier. In a final report released Thursday, the National Transportation Safety Board said the damage went undetected through a scheduled maintenance check and caused a standby rudder control unit to operate abnormally.

The damage came to light after Southwest flight 746 experienced unexpected rudder movements on May 25, 2024, while flying from Phoenix to Oakland, California. All 175 passengers and six crew members were uninjured. The aircraft, registered N8825Q, sustained substantial damage.

The NTSB traced the damage to the night of May 16, when the jet was parked in New Orleans, and thunderstorms brought gusts of up to 73 knots, or about 84 mph. Investigators said the wind likely moved the rudder enough to damage ribs inside the vertical stabilizer where the standby rudder control unit was mounted.

At the time, Boeing’s 737 maintenance manual called for a special inspection after an extreme wind event but gave no wind speed at which the check was required. The manual listed signs such as an aircraft moving over its wheel chocks or leaving tire skid marks.

Southwest also lacked a process to notify maintenance control when a parked aircraft had been exposed to extreme winds. The jet flew the next morning without the inspection.

Over the next week, the aircraft completed 38 flights with no reported rudder or yaw damper problems. It then underwent scheduled maintenance in Houston on May 23, including a test of the standby hydraulic system. The procedure required a mechanic at the tail to verify that the rudder moved in response to pedal inputs.

Hangar video showed the rudder moving to the right but failing to move to the left. Investigators said no one was at the tail to verify the movement. Southwest’s maintenance records showed the test was signed off as passed, and the aircraft returned to service. The NTSB could not determine whether the test worsened the existing damage.

On the fourth flight the next day, a crew disconnected the yaw damper after reporting that it was overcorrecting in turbulence. The yaw damper uses the rudder to counter side-to-side motion.

The jet flew one more leg with the system listed as inoperative. It then passed a functional test, and the yaw damper was returned to service before Flight 746.

On the Oakland flight, the captain noticed momentary stiffness in the rudder pedals while turning onto the runway. Shortly after reaching 34,000 feet, he felt what he described as “a small amount of Dutch roll.” Both pilots felt the pedals move, and the oscillations recurred after the crew descended to 32,000 feet.

Flight data showed one episode of rudder and pedal oscillations lasting about 20 seconds, with no significant change in heading or bank angle. Investigators found that the abnormal movement appeared in the data from the first flight after the Houston maintenance check, before crews reported it. They observed it only when the yaw damper was engaged.

Southwest removed the aircraft from service after it landed in Oakland. The airline later inspected the rudder control unit mounting areas across its 737 MAX fleet and found no similar damage. It also added individual mechanic sign-offs to the hydraulic test and set up a process to alert maintenance control after extreme winds. Boeing revised its maintenance manual to require the special inspection at a wind threshold of 65 knots, or 75 mph.

#6265. Once a Filipino Party Isle, Boracay Has Reinvented Itself

“Fun and sunshine, there's enough for everyone,” says a neon sign before me at the discotheque Club Tropicana on Boracay, a four-square-mile island at the heart of the Philippines. The lyrics are from a buoyant 1983 song, also called “Club Tropicana,” by Wham!. But tonight's playlist is cribbed from the 2010s. As midnight nears, Jennifer Lopez's voice sounds over the speakers, “If you're a party freak, then step on the floor.” So I twirl under a disco ball with gleeful strangers in bikini tops, cargo shorts, and Havaianas flip-flops, beers and gin and tonics in hand.

The effect is transportive. I'm flung 10 years into the past, back when Boracay was the locus of an exuberant, if at times debauched, nightlife scene on the creatively named White Beach. Crowds raved until sunrise and woke up on some of the world's softest sand. They had budget hostels and three-star inns, 24-hour shops, water sports and boats, and eateries of all stripes to keep them entertained until nightfall. Then came the parties, VIP bottle service, and the voice of Kesha speak-singing over sound systems, “Tick-tock on the clock, but the party don't stop, no.”

The thing is, it did. Boracay had to shed its hedonistic streak after a series of closures curtailed tourism. First there was the government-imposed cleanup in 2018 ordered by then president Rodrigo Duterte to correct rampant overdevelopment and environmental negligence. Then there was the COVID-19 shutdown from 2020 to 2022, when the Philippines was closed to foreigners. Boracay lost an estimated $845 million in tourism revenue in 2020 alone and counted only 260,000 visitors. Compare that with 2017, when it raked in roughly $1.1 billion by welcoming more than 2 million travelers who dug their toes into a White Beach clogged with the debris of multiday concerts and ragers thrown by local hosts and corporate mega-sponsors. Broken bottles, cigarette butts, and waste—plastic and otherwise—came in and out with the tides.

The writer (right) aboard a paraw tour at White Beach

Despite growing up in Manila, about an hour away by plane, I never got to see “old” Boracay before immigrating to the United States in 2003. In the 1990s it was beloved for its rustic milieu and unfussy hospitality, though it was already a resort island with more than 100 hotels. My family knew it best in the '80s, when backpackers from Europe and the US began to arrive after the German writer Jens Peters called it, in his 1978 guidebook to the Philippines, “paradise on Earth.” In those halcyon days, paradise had no electricity or potable water. Ice was brought in from the mainland to chill San Miguel Pale Pilsens in Coleman coolers. Even my stepfather, a reluctant traveler, fondly remembers the Boracay of yore: “Your mother and I had only the sea and the stars.”

Boracay is changing yet again. Since 2022 it has vowed to revitalize its economy without sacrificing its environment. Laws now enforce a maximum of 19,000 tourists per day. Smoking, alcohol, littering, single-use plastics, and parties directly on the beach are forbidden. Visitors are not permitted without reservations at accredited lodgings—no more sleeping overnight on the sand. No longer raw as it once was, neither an unspoiled Eden nor a profligate Sodom, this grown-up Boracay is what I've come to see for the first time. As I gaze at the stars above a pristine White Beach, I think, So far, so good.

“Boracay was stuck in a mode,” says entrepreneur Nowie Potenciano as we have brunch at his restaurant Percy Seafood, part of his beachfront hotel Seaworthy Boracay. He's referring to both the island's party animal years and its old culinary scene. Back when sustainability and dairy alternatives weren't yet part of the vernacular, diners usually packed their own food from the cities or bought fresh fish at wet markets to have them grilled or fried at canteens called paluto, meaning “to have something cooked.” They remain part of Boracay's charm today, but now we also have the dishes on our table like mango and tuna ceviche, seafood tagine with prawns and mussels, and grouper marinated in sambal. Dessert is a mélange of coconut-pandan ice cream, mango cubes, and crispy rice from Coco Mama, another Potenciano venture. The entire treat is vegan, and I, lactose intolerant, am grateful.

A seafood platter at Percy Seafood, right on the beach

Pecho, a popular chicken dish at Island Chicken Inasal, served with frozen calamansi

The owner of multiple Boracay restaurants, Potenciano prioritizes sourcing locally. Mahi-mahi and grouper come from nearby Roxas City, oysters from marshy New Washington, and lobsters from the colorful reefs of Palawan. Last October he opened a new restaurant, Hello, Po, inspired by open-fire cooking and smoking traditions from all over the Philippines. As much as possible the ingredients come from Panay, the main island off which Boracay sits. “I want tourists to realize that Boracay is at the center of so much wealth in terms of food and culture,” he says. “It's not just another beach.”

That said, judging it solely as a beach, I get why Boracay is beloved. The sand is soft like confectioners' sugar. The shallows are so vast the waters are basically a giant kiddie pool. Behind a fence of palm trees, all tall and outstretched, as if they're fighting for a cab, there are countless bars, restaurants, canteens, shops, resorts, and hostels. They're divided into “stations” typified by vibe: Station 3, the backpackers haven; Station 2, the busy commercial hub; and Station 1, the home of high-end hotels. Yet wherever your accredited accommodations may be, you can park a blanket anywhere on White Beach. Everyone's welcome to do nothing but sit here and watch the blazing postcard-perfect sunsets.

But I do no such thing. Having missed out on Boracay's previous eras, I am anxious to play catch-up and pack my calendar with activities. While staying at The Lind Boracay, I board a paraw, a traditional outrigger sailboat, and zip along the shore with guides who balance on the watercraft with surprising grace. I go for a snorkeling safari (stunning) and my first try at paddleboarding (nauseating) at the sumptuous Shangri-La Boracay's private Punta Bunga Beach. In the clamorous whirl of D'Mall in Station 2, I shop at the boutique Hiyas, scoring a watch with a pearl bracelet, then grab lunch at Island Chicken Inasal Boracay for grilled birds marinated in calamansi. I have a cocktail at Exit Bar, where a band plays “Easy” (“Easy like Sunday morning…”). After dark the vibe shifts: A handsome, leathery, maybe Swedish DJ busts out his turntables. As I join the crowd untz-ing to the electro-house beat, a fog seems to roll in. It's smoke from cigarettes and vapor from vapes.

Though it leaves me breathless, this rapid-fire succession of capital-E experiences feels natural, like what one is meant to do here. On Boracay the surf shops, tiki bars, karaoke venues, and all-you-can-eat buffets are arranged like dominoes, each address falling into the next. One night I catch a band of dads singing Filipino love songs at Nigi Nigi Nu Noos, a down-home resto-bar with casitas, before I go to Rainbow Cafe and Lounge, where a drag queen performs to a RuPaul song, leaping from a chair and landing in an earth-shaking split. This cornucopia of options can be overwhelming to some and a boon to many. Travelers, alone or otherwise, choose their own adventures and curate vibes by the hour. After decades of being many things to many people, today's Boracay now has everything everywhere all at once.

More people are on the way. Visitor numbers are back to pre-closure levels and only increasing: 2.1 million travelers arrived in 2025, up 3.7 percent from the previous year. To handle them all, a new passenger terminal at Godofredo P. Ramos Airport in Caticlan, the gateway to Boracay, is meant to open in December. Domestic travelers currently outnumber the big spenders from abroad nearly five to one (the split was 50-50 before 2018). But there's still the sense, among business owners I meet, that Boracay is meant to represent the best of the Philippines—not just to foreigners but to ourselves as well.

That's the goal at Subo, a modern Filipino restaurant that straddles Stations 2 and 3. Its chef-owner, Jian Sacdalan, takes guests on a culinary field trip through the country's diverse regions with vegetable pinakbet from Luzon, pork belly pochero from Visayas, and coconut-rich sulu laksa from Mindanao. Subo gets a lot of, as Sacdalan calls them, “intros”—those being introduced to the Philippines for the first time. Staff instruct visitors to leave their flip-flops and Birkenstocks at the entrance. This is a Filipino house after all, and I feel my heart flutter when I'm made to do the same.

“And we get the balikbayans,” Sacdalan says, smiling. Translated literally: country returners, like me. “They long for our culture and heritage, and they get that here.”

When I have breakfast at True Home Hotel, I'm still wet and sandy from spending the already-warm day on White Beach. As co-owner and chef Peter Montemayor hands me Bacolod-style chorizo pudpud, garlic rice, and eggs, he says it's good I'm enjoying the beach. It's what brought him back here after working at resorts in Southeast Asia and the Caribbean: “I said, if I ever return, there's only Boracay.” Another balikbayan.

But Montemayor thinks not enough tourists are relishing White Beach, especially after all that's happened to clean it up. During the 2018 closure True Home Hotel shrank from nine rooms to three to comply with new regulations that forbid permanent structures within 98 feet of the shoreline. He's critical of the government's execution (locals who had to move residences or close businesses weren't supported financially) but admits, “When the island closed, it healed.”

He laments how today's tourists stay dry in the shade, viewing Boracay only through their cameras, or cram their schedules with shopping malls, kiteboarding, windsurfing, and booze cruises where water slides catapult passengers off a ship's stern. “Sounds like my itinerary,” I say, and he laughs. “The island's magic throughout all its iterations,” Montemayor responds, “is how it rewards you when you stand still.”

I taste that peace at Real Coffee and Tea Cafe, a diner in Station 2 styled like a bahay kubo, a stilt house with a thatch roof and bamboo walls. Nearly every surface is covered in sun-bleached photos of guests dating back to when it opened in 1996. The delightfully sour calamansi muffin, it's said, hasn't changed in 30 years. The place feels like a brush with what my family must have longed for: that placid and sweet vibe attached to a Boracay of the past—a contentedness with the here and now.

Inspired to take a breather, I find a spot on White Beach, use my shirt as a blanket, and make to watch the world go by. Instead I drift into a nap. I get to sleep on the sand after all. When I wake, I don't find I've missed out. There's still fun and sunshine. There's enough for everyone.

The pathway over the koi pond at Shangri-La Boracay

The part of White Beach with fewer folks and the softest sand is Station 1, home to Filipino-owned The Lind Boracay. Most of the 118 rooms have sea views, and some have private plunge pools; the brand will come to on-the-rise Philippine island Coron in 2027. The sumptuous Shangri-La Boracay is set on a secluded corner of the island, informally dubbed Station Zero. The 30-acre, 219-key resort has a spa, four restaurants, a PADI-certified water sports center for everything from diving to kitesurfing, and two beaches: the private Banyugan Beach and Punta Bunga Beach, which it shares with sleek Crimson Resort and Spa Boracay and lush Mövenpick Resort & Spa Boracay.

It's easy to fuel up everywhere on the island, especially Station 1: Percy does local seafood dishes; the cocktails at Hello Sailor spotlight Pinoy botanicals; and almost every dessert at Coco Mama is vegan. All are part of the sweet seven-room Seaworthy Boracay. The cozy True Home Hotel and Bistro, with three rooms and an all-day kitchen, is a few doors down. Get a calamansi muffin and an iced latte—there's oat milk—at Real Coffee and Tea Cafe, a 30-year-old oasis amid the hectic vibe of Station 2. In D'Mall, Island Chicken Inasal Boracay serves the titular barbecued bird, one of the region's specialties. At D'Mall's beachside entrance, find Exit Bar for sundowners that become all-nighters. The new Nigi Nigi Too, an eat-drink-and-stay all-in-one, is the latest iteration of a 36-year-old institution. On the border of backpacker haven Station 3 and commercial center Station 2, Subo (meaning “a bite” or “feed”) offers a primer on Filipino regional cuisines. Next door is Boracay Island Brewing Company, with locally made ales on tap.

For a taste of classic Boracay nightlife, hit the dance floors at intimate Club Tropicana, neon-lit Om Boracay, and epic Epic, a storied survivor of the island's closures. If you're looking for a dive-y feel, hit Rainbow Cafe and Lounge for some nibbles and drag shows, and Frendz Resort and Hostel Boracay for a spot of community karaoke (the crowd is young; request some current Top 40).

All of White Beach is yours to claim. Be respectful, do not litter, and leave only footprints.

#6264. Introduction: An Orient Express Adventure Via Africa

Welcome to my next trip report series, covering a trip that I recently wrapped up, which will include reviews of flights and a cruise. This will be a relatively short series, since the trip didn’t last that long, and had a specific purpose. However, as usual, I tried to take an unconventional routing to get to and from the destination, so I could review new experiences.

You can expect reviews of Air Algerie and Royal Air Maroc business class, as well as a review of Orient Express Sailing Yachts, which is Orient Express’ new cruising venture. In this post I’d like to share a basic outline of the trip, and then I’ll have individual review installments in the near future.

The primary reason for this trip was simple, and it was to take a cruise with Orient Express Sailing Yachts. It’s a fascinating time for the luxury cruising industry, and in particular, the increasing number of new lines associated with existing luxury hospitality brands.

Prior to this year, I hadn’t taken a cruise with any cruise line since I was a child, so I’ve been curious to check this all out. At the beginning of the year, I reviewed Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, which was surprisingly lovely, and a very nice reintroduction to cruising.

Then over the summer, I reviewed Four Seasons Yachts, which was definitely upmarket, but had some growing pains.

The newest entrant into this market is Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and arguably it takes luxury cruising to a new level, so you can expect a full review of the experience. Full disclosure — Ford was invited on the sailing (so traveled as a guest of Orient Express) and I tagged along. I’ll still review the experience objectively, of course, but I’ll say upfront that Orient Express simply nailed it, and this matched the feedback Ford has received from clients who have sailed with the company.

Anyway, we sailed with Orient Express Sailing Yachts on a four night journey that started in Marseille, France, and ended in Malaga, Spain, so we needed to position to and from there.

I’m of course always looking for an interesting airline angle when I travel long haul, since my goal is always to try as many new airline products as possible. So rather than flying to Marseille and from Malaga on the “typical” airlines (Air France, British Airways, Lufthansa, etc.), I tried to see if I could instead check some airlines off my list that I’ve been wanting to try. I accomplished that, and below is what my routing looked like.

While I sent Ford direct, I booked a four segment routing for myself, spread across three different tickets.

I had heard a lot about Air Algerie over the years (and not in a good way!), so I decided I finally had to give the carrier a try. Air Algerie typically has very high business class fares, despite the carrier’s lackluster product.

However, I found one decent fare on the carrier’s only route from North America, from Montreal (YUL) to Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, that doesn’t start where I’d like to start, and it doesn’t end where I’d like to end, but that has never stopped me if the price is right. 😉

This included a flight in Air Algerie’s Airbus A330-900neo business class across the Atlantic, and then a connecting flight in Avion Express’ Airbus A320neo business class for the short hop in Africa (this was a wet leased flight operated on behalf of Air Algerie). So I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day) 10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

From there, I of course had to get from Tunis to Marseille (MRS), so I had booked Tunisair’s A320 business class for $270, with the following schedule:

10/04 TU902 Tunis to Marseille departing 1:05PM arriving 3:40PM

Unfortunately I ended up being downgraded shortly before departure due to an aircraft swap. That’s because the flight was swapped to a wet leased Fly2Sky Airbus A320, and I guess they don’t offer business class on those planes. I’m still waiting on any sort of a refund.

Suffice it to say that the outbound wasn’t that smooth, between Air Algerie just royally sucking, and Tunisair downgrading me. I’m happy I had the experience, though!

I should also mention that I had to position to Montreal, so I did that in Air Canada Rouge economy, and flew the following for 11,500 avianca lifemiles plus $54 in taxes & fees:

10/04 AC1651 Miami to Montreal departing 7:55AM arriving 11:28AM

The return portion of our trip was a little more straightforward. Our priority was to get home the same day as our cruise arrived, since we wanted to minimize time away from our kids, and had a family event the next day. So we booked the one routing that would best get us home the same day, which was on Royal Air Maroc, from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN) to Miami (MIA), with the first flight in Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class, and the second flight in Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 787-8 business class.

I booked one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM 10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

On this trip, we just had a single hotel night ahead of our cruise in Marseille (in order to build in a buffer), and we decided to stay at the Hôtel Dieu Intercontinental Marseille. I booked this using an IHG free night award, and it cost 60,000 points before applying the award, so I just had to redeem the difference in points.

I had intended to review the hotel, but I have to apologize, it just didn’t end up working out (since I pride myself in thoroughly reviewing hotels). To be honest, I was dead tired from the journey over, and then we had some drama to deal with back at home most of the afternoon. Then the next morning I prioritized sleeping in, as I was just getting over a cold, rather than getting up at 5AM so I could photograph all parts of the hotel.

So I’m sorry about that. My conclusion is that the hotel has a central location, and from the outside you’d think it’s super charming, but the interior feels mismatched and rather uninspiring and generic.

We had an absolutely amazing time cruising with Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and I was blown away by the experience. What I was less impressed by was my flights to and from Europe, which I routed via Africa in both directions. Air Algerie was downright terrible, while Royal Air Maroc was just unnecessarily bad.

Our Viking guide, Karim Zohny, is leading us through one of the best-preserved ancient temples in all of Egypt, the Temple of Hathor, explaining the famously colorful reliefs that line its massive sandstone pillars, walls and ceilings.

Located along the Nile near the Egyptian city of Qena, it is, as Zohny notes, unusual in its motifs, which include intricate celestial maps and giant images of the Egyptian queen Cleopatra and her son Caesarion.

That our small group of two dozen passengers from the Viking river ship Viking Osiris is even here is also relatively unusual.

Most vessels that sail the Nile don’t come this far north. Instead, they stick to the 130-mile stretch of river that runs between the more southerly cities of Luxor and Aswan.

It's just one of several things that make Viking's 11-night Egypt tours, in my opinion at least (after years of traveling in Egypt), among the best choices for exploring the country's splendors.

Pairing a seven-night Nile sailing with four nights of land-based travel, Viking’s “Pharaohs and Pyramids” trips offer some of the most comprehensive, in-depth touring that you will find in Egypt. They also offer a Nile river ship experience that has few rivals, thanks to Viking’s recent rollout of an all-new series of Nile vessels that is setting a new bar for the region.

In addition, as I have seen on more than one Viking trip in Egypt, the trips offer a particularly seamless and mostly all-inclusive experience, with just about every element — from lodging and meals to expert-led guided tours and special access to iconic sites — included in the fare.

Aimed at the same sort of history-loving travelers who get excited about visiting the ancient ruins of Greece and Italy, Viking’s Egypt trips — like many tours of the country — focus heavily on what some consider the greatest civilization of all time: ancient Egypt.

Indeed, almost from the moment we land in Cairo to begin the tour, which begins with a three-night stay at the upscale Fairmont Nile City Hotel, we are thrust more than 4,500 years back in time to one of the oldest and greatest eras of ancient Egypt: The Old Kingdom.

Also known as the Age of the Pyramids, this was the period that saw the construction of monumental structures such as the 4,700-year-old Step Pyramid of Djoser, which we visit on our first full day of touring.

Located at the edge of the desert just outside Cairo, in an area known as Saqqara, it was, as Zohny explains, not only the first pyramid built in Egypt but also by far the largest stone structure built by humans up to that time.

In that respect, its construction was one of the great milestones of history.

It's a history we experience viscerally as we frog-walk down a low-sloping tunnel into another nearby pyramid built for the pharaoh Teti. After nearly a hundred feet, we emerge into a three-room tomb covered in ancient hieroglyphics, among the oldest funerary texts ever found in an Egyptian tomb.

The next day, Zohny, an expert “Egyptologist” who will be our guide for the entire trip, brings us to the even bigger (and more famous) Pyramids of Giza and the nearby Great Sphinx, which also are just outside of Cairo.

Built about a century after the Step Pyramid of Djoser, the Giza pyramids mark the peak of pyramid building in Egypt and are truly a sight to behold.

In between visiting these massive structures, we are treated to a full morning of exploring the new Grand Egyptian Museum, where we marvel at the gilded treasures recovered from the pharaoh Tutankhamun's tomb just a century ago. We also visit Cairo's alabaster-clad Mosque of Muhammad Ali.

It is a whirlwind two days that prepare us for the equally stunning sites from the more recent New Kingdom, Ptolemaic and Roman periods of ancient Egypt that we will see while sailing the Nile on Viking Osiris.

But first, we must get to the ship. Like most of the vessels that sail the Nile, Viking Osiris is based in Luxor, hundreds of miles south of Cairo — the center of ancient Egypt, which began around 4,100 years ago (when it was called Thebes).

After checking out of the Fairmont, we fly as a group to Luxor on a charter flight.

To sail the Nile on Viking Osiris or one of its many sister vessels (at last count, there were eight on the river) is to be on something akin to a greatest hits tour of nearly 2,000 years of iconic Egyptian structures.

Luxor, Qena, Kom Ombo, Edfu. On the ship's weeklong itineraries, these Nile river destinations famous for ancient sites come one after the other, each offering something spectacular that you probably remember from your second-grade history class.

In Luxor, it is the massive Temple of Karnak, with its colossal sandstone columns arranged in neat rows (if you’ve seen the James Bond vs. Jaws chase scene in the 1977 film “The Spy Who Loved Me,” you know what I’m talking about).

In Qena, it is the impressive Temple of Hathor, which is part of an even bigger archeological site known as the Dendera Temple Complex.

In Kom Ombo, it is the equally impressive temple of the same name, built during the Greco-Roman period and featuring reliefs of the Roman emperors Tiberius and Domitian.

Then there’s Edfu, home to the long-buried-in-sand Temple of Horus. Lost to time until a French archeologist began digging it out 166 years ago, it is almost completely intact, with its hypostyle halls and inner sanctuary looking much as they did 2,000 years ago.

Some of these destinations that the ship visits are gateways to multiple world-class sites. In addition to the Temple of Karnak (where Viking ships have an exclusive dock location), Luxor is our base for an outing to the nearby pharaonic burial grounds, the Valley of the Kings, a highlight of any Egypt tour.

In our case, the visit includes the opportunity to descend into five of the more than 60 tombs found in the valley so far — two more than is typical for many Egypt tours.

Viking has paid extra to get us access to perhaps the most famous tomb of them all, that of the pharaoh Tutankhamun (King Tut, as we called him when I was a boy), who remains inside the tomb in mummified form, as well as the spectacular (and normally expensive to visit) tomb of Seti I.

During our stay in Luxor, we also wandered through the Temple of Luxor and the terraced Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut — the latter a masterpiece of ancient architecture.

Some passengers also soar skyward in a hot air balloon (one of the few extra-charge excursions during the trip) for views of the Mortuary Temple, Valley of the Kings and other area sites from the air.

While exploring the remnants of ancient Egypt is a big part of the trip, it’s not the only focus. As we sail the Nile, we also get a taste of everyday life on the river.

Some of my favorite moments of the voyage come as we steam through the many rural stretches of the Nile between Luxor and Aswan, where the riverbanks often are lined with date palms, reeds, wild grasses and, in some areas, lush agricultural crops.

It is a scene evoking the Nile of ancient times.

At times, I spot farmers working in small fields of bananas or sugarcane, or tending to cows grazing along the waterfront.

We regularly pass fishermen in small boats slapping the water with oars to scare the fish into nets — a traditional technique.

It is, notably, a narrow band of abundance. In some places, the fertile area fed by the life-giving waters of the Nile stretches just a few hundred feet inland, in other places maybe a mile or two, before the landscape abruptly transforms into harsh desert that stretches for hundreds of miles.

It’s one of the things that makes Egypt so fascinating. It is a country that essentially unfolds along one very long, very narrow ribbon of green in a sea of desert.

Or, as the Greek historian Herodotus famously wrote, Egypt is the gift of the Nile.

You can read about this in books, of course. But it's something you only truly understand when you see it up close from the deck of a passing vessel.

One of the big allurements of Viking sailings on the Nile is their laid-back pace.

Many Egypt tour itineraries include only three or four nights of cruising between Luxor and Aswan to see the major sites, or even fewer, resulting in a frenetic touring schedule. There is a lot to pack into just a few days.

Viking is one of just a small number of Egypt tour companies that slow the Nile-cruising portion of the trip by spreading it over a seven-night span. This allows for not only a more in-depth experience but also a more relaxed one — the latter of which has particular appeal to the mostly older travelers who are Viking's core market.

Many of Viking's customers are retirees who have the time for longer trips and also prefer to "explore the world in comfort," as Viking likes to say.

On several days of the sailing, notably, we only tour ancient sites for a few hours in the morning and spend the afternoon relaxing on board as the vessel sails the river.

During this time, Zohny and two other onboard Egyptologists lecture on topics such as medicine in ancient Egypt and Egyptian hieroglyphics. There are lessons in Egyptian cooking and basic Arabic. There's afternoon tea.

But there’s also plenty of time to just kick back on the sun deck.

The extra days also allow time for visits to ancient sites that most tours don’t include and for experiencing more on land than just ancient sites.

In addition to stopping at lesser-visited Qena to see the Temple of Hathor, for instance, we spend a morning docked in the often overlooked Nile town of Esna to see not just its lovely if small Roman-era Temple of Khnum but to shop in one of its small markets for local textiles.

For many of us, the shopping time allows us to haggle for Egyptian galabeyas — a traditional, loose-fitting robe worn by men and women across Egypt — for another major moment of the cruise, that night’s Taste of Egypt & Galabeya Evening. Passengers are encouraged to wear local dress, as the crew does, too, for a special dinner of all-local cuisine, and local music and entertainment.

In Aswan, which is as far south as river ships on these itineraries can go, we spend two days experiencing a wide variety of activities that range from touring the dedicated-to-Isis Temple of Philae and sailing in a traditional wind-powered felucca to visiting one of the local villages that are home to Nubians — a distinct ethnic group that has been living in the region for thousands of years.

We also visit the mighty 56-year-old Aswan High Dam, a marvel of construction that blocks river ships from going farther south on the Nile.

As noted above, Viking Osiris is part of a new series of Viking vessels on the Nile that, in my opinion, are the best-designed on the river.

Upscale and intimate, with just 41 cabins and suites apiece, these vessels feature the same elegant, clean-lined Scandinavian-influenced décor that can be found on Viking ships around the world and lots of high-end touches.

Public areas on each vessel include a stylish restaurant overseen by a European chef, a casual deck-top eatery with indoor and outdoor seating, and a cozy lounge and bar — all offering commanding views.

A key element of the design is the wide expanses of clear glass that serve as the outward-facing walls of nearly every public room. This essentially turns the entire ship into a window onto the stunning, colorful scenery that is scrolling by.

In essence, the light-greenish water of the Nile, the rich green papyrus and tall bamboo-like grasses along its banks, and the tan desert cliffs in the distance become the "art" and focal points of the ship's spaces.

That the glass is clear is notable for the Nile, where many vessels are wrapped in dark or metallic glass to reflect the often-intense heat of the sun — glass that, alas, often makes these ships feel closed off to the splendors of the river. Viking went to great lengths to keep the view clear by sourcing a more expensive type of glass that blocks heat without appearing tinted from the inside — a seemingly small detail that makes all the difference.

Other public spaces on each ship include a swanky sun deck with rows of plush lounge chairs for sunning and lovely shaded seating areas. At the very back of the top deck is a narrow pool.

Even the smallest cabins on the ships are generous in size, measuring 232 square feet. And they are filled with luxury elements such as high-end linens and pillows on the beds, heated bathroom floors and roomy wardrobes with wooden hangers.

My cabin — one of eight suites measuring 409 square feet or more — was among the most luxurious that I have seen on a Nile ship. Modern and residential in feel, it featured a large living room with a seating area and desk for working, an adjacent bedroom with a walk-in closet and bathroom, and an outdoor balcony with seating for two. The latter is something you don't always see on Nile ships.

Still, perhaps the most upscale touch of the vessel is the service level that it offers. A crew of 48 people is on hand to serve at most 82 passengers (the ship's maximum capacity with every cabin full — on my sailing, there were just 72), so there's never a lack of staff to cater to your every whim.

I saw this high service level firsthand quite a few times on board, whether it be from the waiter in the restaurant who, unprompted, prepared my traveling companion a special soothing tea with ginger, lime and honey after she mentioned she was feeling a little queasy, to the bartender in the lounge who not only remembered my favorite cocktail but started mixing it before I even had to ask.

In addition, Zohny, our Egyptologist, was the most knowledgeable and engaging Egypt guide that I have encountered during 25 years of visiting the country.

As is typical for higher-end tours of Egypt, Viking's trips in the region aren't inexpensive.

Sold as a combined land-and-cruise tour package, the 11-night "Pharaohs and Pyramids" journeys start at $6,999 per person, based on double occupancy (about $14,000 for a couple sharing a room). And such starting fares are specifically for packages that include an entry-level "standard" cabin without a balcony during the cruise portion of the trip.

For a package that includes a cabin with a balcony during the cruise portion of the trip, you'll find starting rates of around $7,499 per person (about $15,000 per couple). Packages that include a stay in a larger suite cost closer to $25,000 per couple or more, depending on the departure date.

In general, you'll also pay more at all cabin levels for departures from late December through early April, when cooler temperatures in Egypt make touring more pleasant.

That said, such fares are highly all-inclusive. Not only are your ship and hotel rooms included in the price, but most of your meals (along with wine, beer and soft drinks with lunch and dinner while on the ship). You also get extensive guided tours to all the main sites every day of your trip. The latter is a significant value, given the cost and logistical headaches of booking tours in Egypt on your own.

Indeed, a notable part of what you're paying for on a Viking trip to Egypt is access to extremely knowledgeable Egypt experts (known as Egyptologists) who travel with you and explain the many ancient temples, tombs and other historic sites you're seeing.

In addition, the fares include the interior flights in Egypt that will get you between Cairo and Luxor for the cruise portion of the trip, as well as airport transfers when you book international flights through Viking.

Some higher-level cabins also come with complimentary laundry service and a premium beverage package. Little things like shipboard WiFi are also included for all.

Viking's 11-night "Pharaohs and Pyramids" tours offer one of the most comprehensive and seamless ways to explore Egypt. The trips pair a well-paced, seven-night Nile sailing aboard an exceptionally designed new ship with a multi-night land stay in Cairo, together allowing visits to many of Egypt's most iconic attractions, including the Pyramids of Giza and the Valley of the Kings.

While fares are on the higher side among Egypt tours, the extensive all-inclusive nature of the trips — accommodations, most meals, extensive touring with an expert Egyptologist and internal flights are among the inclusions — means they offer a lot of value for the money. And perhaps most importantly, they make touring Egypt easy.

#6262. The 7 Airlines Flying Airbus A321XLRs On Both Short & Long-Haul Routes

In evolutionary biology, conversation is often focused on 'the' thing features evolved for. For example, bird wings evolved for flying. In reality, birds will use them for whatever they can. Penguins use them for swimming, while chickens use them for changing direction while running and shading their chicks.

Aircraft are somewhat similar. They may be optimized for a specific mission, but that doesn't mean they will be used for those missions by the airline all the time. In Vietnam, VietJet sometimes flies its widebody A330s on ultra-short domestic routes from Ho Chi Minh City to Nha Trang half empty. VietJet apparently does this because the time slot is available in the A330's international schedule.

The Airbus A321XLR is optimized for longer, but thinner routes. On shorter routes, its increased weight from its extra tanks and strengthened landing gear imposes a penalty. Even so, some airlines will operate them on short routes, partly because they are available. Let's examine some of the airlines using the XLR on both short and longer-haul routes.

Aer Lingus is the flag carrier of Ireland and has a fleet of six Airbus A321XLRs. These are configured with 16 business class seats and 168 economy class seats for a total of 184 seats. This is identical to its complementary fleet of eight A321LRs. In July 2026, Aer Lingus flew more than 300 flights longer than 3,100 miles (5,000 kilometers) and more than 200 routes shorter than 1,250 miles (2,000 kilometers) with its XLRs.

Those shorter routes are European hops when the aircraft are not flying their longer transatlantic trips. An example of a long Aer Lingus XLR flight is Dublin to Nashville, which comes with a scheduled flight time of nine hours and 20 minutes. Meanwhile, during the first week of November, the XLR (registered EI-XLU) has flown hops such as Dublin to London (48 minutes) and Dublin to Barcelona (one hour and 50 minutes).

Flightradar24 shows EI-XLU's longer recent flights include Nashville (Tennessee), Cleveland (Ohio), Toronto (Canada), Indianapolis (Indiana), and New York. Being located at the far western edge of Europe, Aer Lingus has the advantage of being able to reach more destinations in the US with the XLR. The XLR is an excellent aircraft for thinner transatlantic missions, but it is also ok to use on short hops, accepting a modest penalty.

Iberia was the launch customer for the Airbus A321XLR in late 2024, and today it operates a fleet of seven examples with an eighth on order. These are configured with 14 business class seats and 168 economy seats, totaling 182 seats. Spain (excluding Russia) leads Europe with the most domestic flights, driven by the need to connect the mainland with the Canary Islands and Balearic Islands.

From its base in Madrid, Iberia flies its A321XLRs to transatlantic destinations in the United States such as Boston, Newark, Washington DC, and Canada's Toronto. Having a more Spanish and Latin focus than carriers like the UK or Ireland, it also flies them to the Dominican Republic (Santo Domingo) and Puerto Rico (San Juan) in the Caribbean (both Spanish-speaking).

In South America, its XLRs fly as far as Recife and Fortaleza in Brazil. Recent flight tracking data for the XLR registered EC-OOJ reveals it is mostly flying longer transatlantic routes. However, it has also flown European hops to Zurich and Paris (both one hour and 30 minutes) as well as Venice (two hours).

Qantas will have one of the highest passenger capacities onboard its Airbus A321XLRs.

Air Canada is one of the XLR's newest operators, with the national Canadian airline flying the aircraft since June. Now the airline has a growing fleet of five to six in service. Air Canada's official website says it has six in inventory, while Planespotters.net still records five delivered, of which one is currently grounded. That aircraft is brand new and working up.

Regardless, Air Canada is in the process of building up one of the world's largest XLR fleets, with around 24 of its 30-strong order still to be delivered. Air Canada is using the aircraft on a range of longer routes, including transatlantic flights to Europe. C-GXLR was the first XLR delivered to Air Canada. In recent weeks, its longest flight was Toronto to Copenhagen (up to eight hours),

Other longer routes include Montreal to Toulouse (about seven hours), as well as Montreal to Lisbon, Montreal to Porto, and other European destinations. It is also used extensively on medium (three- to five-hour) flights to various destinations in the United States and western Canada such as Los Angeles and Calgary. Ultra short hops include Ottawa to Toronto (39 minutes) and Montreal to Toronto (53 minutes).

Qantas is another of the leading Airbus A321XLR customers, with a total of 48 on order or delivered. The Flying Kangaroo is currently taking delivery of its XLRs, with seven now in inventory. These are ideally suited to some Pacific routes where the range is vast, but the routes are thin. The fact that Qantas ordered 20 more XLRs in August 2025 suggests it has many Asia-Pacific routes in mind.

However, few have been announced. The XLR registered VH-OGA was the first delivered to Qantas in April 2025. Confusingly, its flight history over the last month shows it has only been used on domestic routes. The shortest route is the one-hour flight between Sydney and Melbourne, while the longest flight is the domestic transcontinental flight from Sydney to Perth, which is less than five hours.

Qantas is introducing the type progressively and assigning it to domestic trunk routes before expanding internationally. Upcoming international routes include Perth to India (expected), Adelaide to Singapore, and Brisbane to Manila. While Qantas has not announced all of its upcoming Pacific routes, interesting destinations include Fiji, Samoa, the Cook Islands, and Tahiti.

American Airlines now has 11 of its 40 XLRs ordered in inventory. As with European carriers, American is assigning these to transatlantic routes. They also have the range to reach many leisure and thinner destinations in the Caribbean, Central America, and South America.

The first XLR American took delivery of is N300NY. Its most recent flight history is dominated by transcontinental routes flying from Boston or New York to Los Angeles or San Francisco, taking around five hours. It is also flying transatlantic routes from New York to Barcelona (up to eight hours) and New York to Edinburgh (up to six hours).

Largest publicly reported A321XLR customers

While short hops appear less common in American's fleet, there are some. One XLR (N301NY) has flown hops like Boston to Philadelphia (one hour). As with other airlines, the American XLR fleet is working up and is yet to take on many of its intended routes. South America is identified as a future market with potential American routes including Miami to Porto Alegre, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, and others.

The Airbus321XLR will change the mid-sized market and allow new destinations for airlines.

United Airlines is another major airline busy inducting its new XLR fleet and gearing up for transatlantic and other routes. It has recently suggested that the XLR lacks the range to serve some deeper European routes, such as those to Greece. This is somewhat confusing, as it is well within the advertised range and other airlines fly comparable distances.

United has not provided a detailed breakdown of its calculations, including payload, required margins, routing, etc., to understand the assertion. It has just received the first three of its 50-strong order, leaving 47 remaining on the order book. These are now starting to replace its aging fleet of 757-200s.

With the first delivered in May, United's XLR remains a fleet in its infancy. Flight records show they have yet to fly longer transatlantic routes to Western Europe, although they are coming. Mostly, the flights have been transcontinental, around four to five hours. One short hop in the record is San Diego to Denver, a flight time of less than two hours.

IndiGo is the leading low-cost carrier of India and is one of the world's fastest-rising carriers. It boasts a fleet of 425 aircraft in service and has 881 more on order. While delivered, that will make it one of the largest airlines in the world in the 2030s. The airline's fleet is overwhelmingly A320 family narrowbodies, although it has 60 A350 widebodies on order.

IndiGo has 175 A321neos in service plus four new XLRs. It has the largest order for the XLR, totalling 69 examples. This is made up of the 40 original firm orders publicly confirmed by IndiGo and 29 additional aircraft reflected in industry fleet databases. Once again, the fleet is in its infancy and is working up.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

With that being said, IndiGo seems much faster at deploying them on its longer-haul routes than other airlines. Flight history for VT-NLA shows it has been flying between Delhi and Athens (over eight hours), Mumbai and Istanbul (over seven hours), Mumbai and Amsterdam (up to nine hours and 30 minutes). One example of a short hop is the two-hour route between Delhi and Mumbai.

#6260. Brisbane Gets Its Moment in the Sun

Late one afternoon last November, Ty Simon works the room at Golden Avenue. He laughs with a pair of men in suits, tops off the glasses for a table of women in flower-patterned dresses, squeezes shoulders, and nods and smiles his way across the rest of the floor. Waiters ferry wine and coffee and platters of hummus and salads between the kitchen and the split-level dining space. Sheets of bright Queensland sun pour in through the open walls. It's Tuesday, it's lunch, and the place is full, unrushed, and lovely; it feels good to be here. Golden Avenue opened in the middle of last year as the ninth restaurant from Simon and his wife, Milan-born Biànca Marchi-Simon, through their Anyday hospitality group, which started with the Asian-inflected Longtime and went on to include Agnes, a dimly lit open-flame spot that won Australia's Restaurant of the Year in 2023. When Simon returns to our table, I remark on the hospitality that I've just seen. “Here we take a community approach,” he says. “My goal has always been to make sure that the people who like us, love us.”

The community approach may be the key to his city's success. Brisbane—Australia's perpetually distant-third city—has long been reduced by the Aussies to a “big country town.” (Their words—not mine!) Though a good-natured and happy place, it lacked the natural beauty and trendsetting of Sydney and the cultish urban creativity of Melbourne. For decades Brisbane seemed to succumb to the belief that it could never compete. It lacked personality in its Central Business District (CBD) and had pretty much no public transport. Even geography worked against it: In a state prized for its coastline, Brisbane is nearly 50 miles from a surf beach. Locals would often zip overseas or migrate south, perhaps on the assumption that their ambition could never be realized at home. The big country town endured.

The astounding Kith and Kin, from Queensland artist Archie Moore, which won the Golden Lion at Venice’s 60th biennale, on display at GOMA

Then a shift began. The city council embarked on an ambitious rebranding in 2010 to position Brisbane as globally connected and dynamic, giving it the nickname of New World City (“It was about shedding the idea of being the poor cousin,” Simon says). The magnificent Gallery of Modern Art (GOMA) had opened just a few years before, attracting world-class works from the Pacific and beyond. The council leveraged the city's billion-dollar location, just north of the booming Gold Coast, with its high-rises and killer beaches, and south of the covetable Sunshine Coast, with the Great Barrier Reef just off its shores. Millions traveled in from all over each year for what lay on either side of Brisbane, so why not make the city bait for some of their money and time? Many Brisbanites, Simon included, began to grow this place together, creating a city that reflected their own ambitions—and themselves. In the 2010s the city developed sharply designed precincts filled with glamour shopping and higher-level dining, all under year-round sunshine and with Brisbane's noticeable good cheer and friendliness. In 2021 the IOC announced that Brisbane would host the summer Olympics in 2032, following Los Angeles.

And right around that same time, COVID hit. While the rest of Australia struggled with lockdown and tight regulations that dragged on, Queensland fared generally well, with looser rules and relatively low numbers of cases after the initial shutdowns. “We had Melburnians coming into Brisbane just to feel normal again,” says entrepreneur and developer Catherine Malouf.

Malouf may be the most recognizable face of Brisbane's new chapter. Her family is one of the key forces behind the James Street precinct, a fig-tree-studded melange of open-air coffee houses, Champagne bars, and high-end restaurants strung together with designer shops selling top local labels. “I wanted to create somewhere where we could have a good lunch, a glass of wine, and go shopping in a place that felt like the best of Australia,” she says as we eat grilled chicken and salads at her Hellenika restaurant. Stylish and elegant, Malouf exudes the kind of sophistication you may more often associate with the places she formerly called home, like Italy and California, but her good nature and easy friendliness is all Brisbane. In a sense she personifies the version of Brisbane she is invested in creating: global and chic but anchored in hometown charm. “It took me 20 years to come back and realize that this is the place I want to live in, and a lot of people have realized that too,” she says. “It is comfortable. It is easy.”

The precinct's architecture is heavy, concrete, and borderline Brutalist, but not at all ugly. It creates an aura of strength and permanence that's almost symbolic for the next chapter of a city whose heritage architecture was mostly knocked down and whose locals have often fled elsewhere for opportunity. And amid it all is the anchor of the precinct, The Calile, an urban resort hotel whose execution feels Aussie but whose ambition and hospitality would work in any major global city. Its opening—along with its smartly designed rooms and mezzanine-level pool, bars, and restaurants that spill over into the general precinct sidewalks—catapulted the James Street precinct onto the radars of international travelers. “We are very much an Aussie hotel, but we are increasingly hosting people from around the world,” Malouf says.

Designer Heidi Middleton inside her atelier, Artclub

The James Street precinct serves as a gateway to Australia. The stores here, high-end and, for the most part, independent, are nearly all Australian brands such as P. Johnson, St. Agni, and Brisbane's own Gail Sorronda. A centerpiece is Artclub, from fashion designer Heidi Middleton, which launched here last year. Like many of her fellow Brisbanites, Middleton left to start and grow a business whose ambitions, she felt, would never flourish in Brisbane. After spending decades in Europe and selling her globally renowned Sass & Bide, she alleviated her homesickness and moved back. Artclub is a sustainably minded fashion brand that focuses on small production and renewable materials. Middleton remarks that the key to the precinct's success is the curation: high-end and never high street. “They have created a genre that is all their own,” she says.

Brisbane is called the River City for the coffee-hued eponymous waterway that snakes through it. Like the James Street precinct, the river, too, has been a focus for a lot of redevelopment. The work here—walkways, bridges, cycling and jogging lanes, dining districts, and green spaces—has pulled the city together and been a catalyst for a revamped relationship between people and place. On the banks near the James Street precinct, where a once industrial wasteland lay abandoned and uninspired, now sits the reimagined Howard Smith Wharves, alive with breweries, green parks, and restaurants. It's located on the Brisbane Riverwalk, a network of overwater walkways that are dotted with bright red royal poinciana flame trees, which didn't exist 10 years ago. Along the walk sits Stanley, an excellent Chinese spot that conjures a Hong Kong evening parlor and was opened by Louis Tikaram, who made a name on the global culinary stage as executive chef of EP & LP in West Hollywood. A 15-minute stroll away is Supernormal, the only sister restaurant to the hit Melbourne joint of the same name, whose 2024 opening unofficially announced Brisbane as a serious foodie city.

A signature steamed dumpling basket from Stanley

Four new pedestrian bridges have opened to decrease car traffic, promote sustainable living, and solve some of the city's connectivity issues. The latest, Kangaroo Point Bridge, connects the suburb of Kangaroo Point to the CBD, and it's bookended with coffee bars and has green spaces so that pedestrians can relax while looking out over the water. Zigzagging underneath them all is the beloved CityCat ferry, which zips from bank to bank, chartering passengers throughout town and beyond. Stops include the wonderful South Bank cultural district, where you'll find GOMA and the Queensland Art Gallery (QAG). It chugs its way to West End, Brisbane's perennial counterculture neighborhood, which has a funky retro cinema, indie shops selling Japanese crafts and fashion, and solid food.

Take the ferry north and you'll arrive at Brisbane Powerhouse. A hulking industrial building that powered the city starting in the 1920s, it was reborn in 2000 as the city's contemporary art center, complete with sprawling grounds, rooftop areas, bars, restaurants, and untouched industrial spaces that can host interactive exhibitions. It's raw and cool, and its scale is enormous. When I meet Louise Bezzina there, she is in her second week as the Powerhouse's artistic director and CEO. Kind and unassuming, she is the type of person you might casually meet at a mutual friend's birthday dinner and, 15 minutes into the conversation, realize you are sitting next to someone brilliant. “As Australia develops it allows for more cities to grow—it is not just Sydney and Melbourne,” she says. “Brisbane has long been an untapped city of opportunity.”

She is part of the cohort of local leaders drilling into its potential. Prior to the Powerhouse, Bezzina was the creative director of Brisbane Festival, the largest international festival in Australia by attendance numbers, for which she secured the Jean Paul Gaultier show over creative capitals like Melbourne in 2024. “My edgy style suits Brisbane,” she believes. For her first project at the Powerhouse, she launched “Swingers: The Art of Minigolf,” an interactive statement on female empowerment in a male-dominated world, pegged to the origin story of the putting game, which was founded in the 19th century by Scottish women who had been banned from 18-hole golf on account of their gender; each of the nine holes here was designed by a different female-identifying artist. Bezzina has begun ideating plans to partner with Los Angeles and Pacific dance groups in the lead-up to (and handoff of) the Summer Olympic Games.

But to suggest that creativity is new to Brisbane would be misleading. Designer Lydia Pearson is a local loyalist who has long believed in the power of her hometown. “It used to be that if you wanted to be successful, you had to either leave or create it yourself,” she says. She chose the latter. In 1989 Pearson cofounded the fashion brand Easton Pearson with fellow designer Pamela Easton, which focused on circular fashion through textiles and hand embroidery. It took off, showing during Paris Fashion Week in 1999 and selling in 20 countries before the label closed in 2016. The following year the Museum of Brisbane acquired more than 3,000 pieces from the Easton Pearson archive and has put some of the items on permanent display. “The hard part was getting people to believe you could make a brand in Brisbane that wasn't simply a hibiscus-patterned dress,” Pearson says.

We meet in the leafy suburb of Red Hill, where she and her current partner, the artist Shilo Engelbrecht, work diligently to upcycle old fabrics into a new life through their label, ShiloLydia. This could mean turning an antique tablecloth into a sheer, soft dress, or reworking discarded linens into sharp shirts whose silhouettes could compete with any on a global catwalk. The work is slow, careful, and considered—a preservation effort as much as it is a creative one. The results are delicate and beautiful, a quiet and enduring counter to the louder creativity happening across the city.

Their studio sits inside a Queenslander, an old, iconic style of house that started to appear in Brisbane in the mid-1800s. The structures are wood, often colorful but always fragile, with large verandas designed to catch and route cooling breezes through the home. Queenslanders are delightful and charming, and have become recognizable to millions of viewers around the world who tune into Brisbane's most famous export, Bluey. The beloved animated show about Bluey, a blue heeler dog, who is likely known to more people around the world than her real-life fellow Brisbanite Jacob Elordi, is the creation of animator Joe Brumm. The show airs in 28 languages and more than 140 countries. For several years it was the most streamed show in the United States of any genre, and it has an empire worth $2 billion. Brisbane is a main character, and the city is unmistakable via the iconic Queenslander wood homes, the ibis birds pecking around, the sun and steep hills, the hours of imaginative outdoor play that Brumm says is modeled after his own upbringing in Queensland. Bluey resonates with parents and children of the world due to the heart and the humor at the show's core, something Brumm says defines Brisbane. “It is about the cheer that I feel when I come back,” he says. A good reminder, then, that a place's most resonant selling point is often something that can't be built.

True urban resort The Calile Hotel helped put Brisbane on the traveler map. The hotel has a phenomenal pool and fitness space; even if you're not staying here, swing by for its Lobby Bar and excellent restaurants, including Hellenika, which serves Greek favorites.

Inside a restored heritage Queenslander, the intimate Spicers Balfour Brisbane is well-located in New Farm: It's walking distance from the James Street precinct, the Howard Smith Wharves, and Brisbane Powerhouse.

The dimly lit, decidedly grown-up restaurant Agnes, which was named Australia's Best in 2023, is known for its exceptional wood-fired cooking of duck, steak, and more.

Housed inside a former church in West End, August is a nod to the reverence of Sunday lunch, with considerately prepared plates of Noosa snapper and Jerusalem artichoke risotto.

Sleek and light-flooded, the 15-month-old Middle Eastern spot Golden Avenue has great eggplant and grilled meats.

Do an outdoor table and load it up with all the dumplings and noodles you can order at superb riverside restaurant Stanley that feels like high-end Hong Kong parlor dining.

The Brisbane outpost of the hot Melbourne restaurant Supernormal has a glamorous dining room with large water-facing windows and a fun, Asian-inflected menu that leads with local produce and protein.

Located near the funky Fish Lane, Southside is the spot for dumplings and siu mai after strolling the museums of South Bank.

The French Exit, the newest venture from Ty and Biànca at Anyday, has Parisian-style interiors by star designer Tamsin Johnson and cool bars and dining rooms spread over multiple floors in a heritage building.

Brisbane's cultural hub is South Bank, with Gallery of Modern Art (GOMA) and other institutions featuring Indigenous, Australian, and Pacific Island artists. The riverfront Brisbane Powerhouse has ambitious and edgy festivals, exhibitions, and events throughout the year.

For the best Australian labels, head to the James Street precinct for objects from Dinosaur Designs; stylish dresses from St. Agni; and sustainable, one-off fashions from Heidi Middleton's atelier, Artclub. Over in Red Hill, drop into ShiloLydia as well as the other ateliers that share space in the same Queenslander. Shilo Engelbrecht also hosts collage and meditation workshops in her studio out back by appointment.

The best way to see (and travel) Brisbane is the CityCat ferry, which bounces between 22 stops along the river. But the city has made walking easier too. Stroll the overwater footpaths on the waterfront up to the gorgeous City Botanic Gardens. If you‘re keen for a longer walk after checking out the exhibitions at GOMA, find your way to West End for funky vintage shopping and phenomenal food.

There is no shortage of worthy weekend getaways from Brisbane, including the Gold Coast and Noosa on the Sunshine Coast. But drive an hour inland to the artsy, beautiful Tamborine Mountain for a lovely look at a lesser-explored side of Queensland. Stay at the chic, two-year-old Tamborine Boutique Hotel, where a pantry and bar stock local snacks. Have lunch at the petite Picnic Real Food Bar, and don't worry if it's already run out of the plump and delicious pies (everything is worth trying). Then head around the corner for local amaro tastings at Loborn. Restore yourself after mountain hikes at the floating Sol Elements spa, whose soaking baths and salt room all seem to hover over a lake.

#6259. Which Airlines Fly To The Most Countries? One Carrier Has A Huge Lead

I don’t want to bury the lede — in posts, I often reference how Turkish Airlines flies to more countries than any other airline in the world. However, how many countries does the airline actually fly to, and how far ahead of competitors is Turkish Airlines? I thought that would be interesting to explore…

Turkish Airlines has the record for flying to more countries than any other airline in the world. That has been the case for a long time, and in late 2024, the Star Alliance carrier made it official, with a Guinness World Record in the category of “most countries flown to by an airline.” The airline has flown to more countries than any other airline since 2012, and has a sizable lead over competitors.

Just how many countries does Turkish Airlines fly to? This is where it always gets tricky as to what you count. If you count active flights operating at the moment, the airline flies to 117 countries. However:

As you’d expect, when you’re an airline serving virtually every corner of the globe, there will always be some suspended services due to geopolitical factors, etc. What’s cool is that Turkish Airlines is also far from done with its expansion, as the airline still has big growth plans. It’ll be fascinating to see just how many countries the airline eventually serves.

What’s perhaps most impressive about Turkish Airlines’ record for serving the most countries is just how far ahead of competitors the airline is. Turkish Airlines is 30+ countries ahead of the next airline when it comes to countries served.

Does anyone want to take a guess as to which airlines are next on the list? Here are a few general thoughts that come to mind:

With that in mind, which airlines serve the most countries, aside from Turkish Airlines? According to flightconnections.com, here are some observations:

As you can see, that means Qatar Airways serves the most countries after Turkish Airlines, while Air France, British Airways, and Ethiopian Airlines, are currently tied for third place.

Meanwhile it’s impressive that Emirates serves so many countries when you consider that the airline just flies wide body jets. If you combined the networks of Emirates and flydubai (both are owned by the government, but the airlines are run separately), then the combined airline would have close to as many destinations as Turkish Airlines.

Let me of course also acknowledge that the number of countries served and number of destinations served is very different, and US carriers would do much better by the latter metric. And if the question is the number of premium destinations served, then there’s only one right answer. 😉

When you put it all together, below is the chart with the 13 most “global” airlines, in terms of countries served (I had to include KLM as well, since it ties Air Canada and Delta, even if it doesn’t lead the way among European carriers).

Turkish Airlines sets the world record for serving the most countries in the world. The airline actively flies to 117 countries, but including suspended routes, serves 130+ countries. That puts the airline way ahead of the next carriers by this metric, which include Qatar Airways at 86 countries, followed by a tie between Air France, British Airways, and Ethiopian Airlines, at 80 countries.

Are you surprised by the airlines serving the most countries?
