Annual passes to major U.S. theme parks like Walt Disney World, Universal Orlando Resort, SeaWorld and Legoland come with a long list of benefits. You can visit as often as you like; you get discounts on extras like parking, merchandise and dining; and your pass often comes with access to special events throughout the year.

Theme park annual passes also come with a hefty price tag that can climb upward of $1,000. Because of this, it can be easy to assume an annual pass is only worth the cost if you live near one of these parks and can visit every week.

As an out-of-state resident who has held an annual pass to Universal Orlando Resort since 2020, I can assure you that assumption is incorrect. But you don't have to take my word for it.

I calculated the break-even point for 10 theme parks across the country to help you decide whether it's an option worth looking into. For consistency, I based these calculations on each park's top-tier pass and the lowest one-day ticket prices, using park-to-park tickets at resorts with multiple parks, since annual passes include park-to-park access.

Because these calculations are based on one-day tickets, you would still need to determine whether you could save money with an annual pass by considering the ticket cost on the date(s) of your visit (most parks have variable pricing), how many trips you take each year and the number of days you visit per trip.

**About 6 once you factor in the cost of free parking and the Express passes

Disney World offers several annual passes, but only one, the Disney Incredi-Pass, is available to out-of-state residents. The Disney Incredi-Pass has no blockout dates and includes complimentary theme park parking.

If you were to visit only on the cheapest days of the year, you would need to visit nine times each year to realize the value of a Disney World annual pass as a non-Florida resident. When you factor in shopping and dining discounts and free parking, you can probably break even after eight visits. But if you were to visit on the more expensive days, you could break even in closer to six days.

Related: Bluey, Buzz and Grogu: Opening dates for new Disney World and Disneyland attractions in 2026

Remember, though, this comparison is based on the one-day ticket price. If you plan to spend eight days at Disney World broken up between one or two visits per year, you could potentially do better to buy a multiday park hopper ticket versus an annual pass. Because Disney uses variable ticket pricing and tickets get less expensive as you add more days, you have to do the math to find out which is best for you.

Don't worry, the math on most other parks isn't quite as involved.

Disneyland's top-tier pass is called the Inspire Key. At $1,899 per year, this pass has blackout dates during the weeks of Christmas and New Year's Eve, and it includes free standard parking and unlimited Disney PhotoPass downloads.

The Inspire Key pass can pay for itself after 11 visits, since the lowest park hopper tickets start at $179.

Related: How Disneyland's newest ride proves that 'progress is impossible without change'

As with Disney World, the number of visits required to break even would decrease if you visited on more expensive days, and you could still save money by purchasing multiday tickets.

Universal Orlando has several annual pass options, but the 2-Park Premier Pass is the easiest to use and has the most benefits. You get park-to-park admission between Universal Studios Florida and Universal Islands of Adventure, complimentary skip-the-line Express passes after 4 p.m., complimentary valet and prime parking, one free ticket to Halloween Horror Nights, early park admission and several valuable discounts.

If you were to visit during the holidays when one-day park-to-park tickets climb as high as $255, you can break even after four days. It's also worth doing the calculations with the included Halloween Horror Nights ticket, which starts at $99. When you factor that in, you can break even after five visits.

Related: Epic Universe tips: 11 ways to spend less time in line and have more fun

A six-day park-to-park ticket that also includes access to Universal Epic Universe is only $550.99 per person, so if you only plan to visit once per year for six days, you would save significantly by purchasing a multiday ticket versus an annual pass.

Universal Studios Hollywood only has one park, making the math here easier to calculate. The park's Platinum Annual Pass has no blockout dates and includes free general parking most of the year, one Halloween Horror Nights ticket and Express skip-the-line access after 3 p.m.

You'd technically have to visit 6.0025 times to break even, but if you include the free parking and after-3 p.m. Express passes, we can safely say you break even after six visits.

Related: Thrills for all ages: 6 best rides at Universal Studios Hollywood

Similar to Universal Orlando, you can break even sooner if you factor in the cost of a Halloween Horror Nights ticket, which starts at $77 per person. When you factor that in, plus those other perks, you can break even after approximately five one-day visits.

This is where things get a little bit fun (in my opinion, anyway). Legoland's Premium Annual Pass includes visits to more than 20 Merlin attractions across the country, including Legoland, Peppa Pig Park, Sea Life Aquarium, Madame Tussauds wax museum and more. A lot of these parks are in theme park hubs like Florida, California and Texas, so you likely aren't too far from one or multiple locations.

In this case, you don't need to plan multiple visits to a single park to see the value in an annual pass. You can visit multiple locations around the country with no blockout dates, free parking and four free "Bring-a-Friend" tickets (one ticket per quarter), which make the math very appealing.

If you assign a $69 value to the "Bring-A-Friend" tickets, four per year would equal $276, just $23 less than the total annual pass cost. So, if you were to visit one of the 20+ parks nationwide four times per year (once per quarter) and bring a friend or family member with you, you'd save money with an annual pass before even factoring in free parking and other discounts.

This is another instance where you can access multiple parks with a single annual pass. SeaWorld Orlando's Platinum Pass includes unlimited admission to 11 parks across the country with no blockout dates. These include all SeaWorld and Busch Gardens parks, as well as their affiliated water parks. You also get eight free guest tickets, free photos and free preferred parking.

A few notes here. You can't use all eight free guest tickets at the same time and they are limited to select parks. SeaWorld allows you to use a certain number of tickets during different calendar windows throughout the year. But if you were to visit these parks eight times per year and bring a friend, you would save more than $600 by purchasing an annual pass.

It's also worth noting that SeaWorld San Diego's Platinum Pass is only $201 on sale, and its lowest one-day ticket costs $64.99, so you'd break even after just four visits. While it provides the passholder access to the same 11 parks, its guest passes can only be used at the California parks.

Opened in July 2026, Universal Kids Resort is the newest park on this list. The park recently started selling annual passes, with the Gold Annual Pass being its top-tier offering. The Gold pass has no blockout dates and includes regular self-parking.

Assuming you visit on five separate days and only visit on the least expensive days, you would break even after five visits. But because the Gold Pass also includes free parking and other discounts, you could potentially break even in four one-day visits. Because the park also sells discounted multiday tickets, the above math only makes sense if you were to visit on five nonconsecutive days.

You don't need to live in Florida or California to have access to award-winning theme parks. Holiday World in Santa Claus, Indiana, consistently wins awards for its cleanliness, water park and thrilling coasters. Holiday World's Platinum Pass has no blockout dates, early entry for select attractions and discounted "Bring-a-Friend" tickets.

Holiday World already offers free parking, sunscreen and soft drinks, so you won't get additional discounts there. You would break even after four one-day visits, assuming you purchase the lowest-cost tickets.

Dollywood's top-of-the-line pass is a Diamond Season Pass (a very fitting name for our bright and shining queen Dolly Parton, if you ask me). With it, you get unlimited visits, complimentary parking, Time Saver skip-the-line access for the first hour of each day, a 20% discount on shopping and dining, and four free "Bring-a-Friend" tickets.

Dollywood handles its "Bring-a-Friend" tickets differently. You can use them one at a time or all four at once. If you brought four friends with you during your first visit after buying your annual pass, you would have more than covered the cost of your pass. In fact, you could save about $110 by purchasing an annual pass instead of five one-day tickets (you and four friends). Any future visits that year are just a bonus. Just one of the million reasons to love Dollywood.

Silver Dollar City and Dollywood are owned by the same parent company (Herschend Family Entertainment), but their annual passes work quite differently. Silver Dollar City's Diamond Pass includes unlimited visits to the park and White Water water park, eight free "Bring A Friend" tickets (to be used during specific redemption windows at Silver Dollar City or White Water), a bonus "Bring-a-Friend" ticket you can use on any day and $29.99 tickets for friends and family.

Even though you can't use all of your "Bring-a-Friend" tickets at one time, you only need to visit with a guest twice to break even with an annual pass before even digging into the savings you would find from in-park discounts.

In addition to the advertised benefits, there is a level of convenience that comes with being a passholder. You can pop in for a few hours without feeling like you wasted money on a full-day ticket, and you feel like a more valuable guest when you visit. I often get things like priority parade seating, fun freebies and passholder-only discounts of up to 70% off merchandise.

No amount of math matters unless you know you will actually use and enjoy the benefits of being a passholder. Use these calculations as a jumping-off point to decide if you are ready to be a passholder.

#6257. Why You Should Pack Your Hiking Boots on a Trip to St. Croix

The smell hit me out of nowhere: an uncanny whiff of sweaty socks. I instinctively glanced around for another hiker. My guide, local naturalist Olasee Davis, laughed and pointed to a thick brown seed pod lying on the trail. It had fallen from a West Indian locust, more commonly known as a stinking toe tree.

The culprit loomed farther down the trail, its massive limbs weaving a vaulted canopy overhead. “It tastes better than it smells,” Olasee said, picking up the pod and cracking it open on a rock to reveal the powdery pulp inside. I watched him take a bite but decided to pass. I suspected stinking toe fruit was an acquired taste, and with only a few days remaining on my trip to St. Croix, I'd save the acquiring for a future visit.

As we continued along, Olasee introduced me to other tropical evergreens, including the soursop, laden with spiky fruit, and the red manjack, much shorter and shrubbier, with brownish-red berries. Around the next bend he pointed out nonnative fruit trees: papaya from South America and mango from India. But he hadn't brought me here just for the botany. He'd brought me to understand why this forest matters.

As an ecologist, historian, and assistant professor at the University of the Virgin Islands, Olasee helped lead the effort to establish Maroon Sanctuary Territorial Park in 2025. Encompassing 2,469 acres in the northwest corner of St. Croix, the park protects part of Maroon Country, the island's steep, forested interior where people who had escaped slavery found refuge during the 1700s and early 1800s. The new park also safeguards former sugar plantations and mill sites, which have been slowly returning to nature since Denmark ended slavery in the Danish West Indies (present-day US Virgin Islands) in 1848. By that time more than 100,000 enslaved Africans had passed through the port of Christiansted on St. Croix, the largest of the islands, to be sold to plantation owners in the Danish Caribbean sugar economy.

Olasee and I were following an old plantation trail through one such former estate when he suddenly stopped and then scrambled up a steep embankment into the trees. I followed, brushing aside slender branches. Hidden beneath the understory, almost swallowed by spider lilies, was a burial ground. Most graves were marked with conch shells. Some were covered by low, weathered concrete slabs. One was marked by a headstone, its inscription softened by decades of moisture and lichen. The hidden cemetery wasn't an isolated discovery. For more than 40 years, Olasee has bushwhacked his way through Maroon Country to search for burial grounds and other traces of those who escaped slavery, documenting sites that would otherwise disappear beneath the forest. Now that it's been conserved as a territorial park, that work can continue in a more systematic, permanent way. Or as Olasee put it, “I could die in peace now.”

Travelers have traditionally come to the USVI for beach vacations and sailing charters; now Maroon Sanctuary is opening up another side to the islands. The park's founders are also building out an official trail network. The roughly 10 miles of trail that I explored with Olasee were a patchwork of former estate roads, plantation footpaths, and forgotten forest routes that he'd pieced together over decades. Soon these trails will be easier to navigate without needing someone like Olasee to lead the way. The next morning I met Kristina “Kitty” Edwards, director of the US Virgin Islands Division of Territorial Parks & Protected Areas, at a trailhead on the slopes of 1,165-foot Mount Eagle, the island's highest peak. We were about to hike the first official segment of the trail, a three-mile loop designed for hiking and mountain biking, which opened this past May. When completed, the trail system will wend 30 miles through the forested backcountry.

As excited as Kitty was to show off the new path, a first of its kind on the island, she wasn't in a hurry. “I'm a meanderer,” she said with a shrug and a smile. In the shirt-soaking heat of the tropics, I was grateful to take it slow. We ascended amid white-winged butterflies and yellow-breasted bananaquits. After an hour we reached the stone remnants of the old watchtower that marked the summit. A spur trail led us to an overlook where we paused to take in the 270-degree view, bookended by emerald peaks to our right and the inviting turquoise waters of Cane Bay to our left. It occurred to me that Maroon Sanctuary wasn't just about the land. The park's protected boundary extends all the way to the sea, helping shield Cane Bay's coral reefs and the nearby Annaly Bay tide pools from pollution and sediment.

A green sea turtle in the warm waters around St. Croix

I spent the next day reveling in those crystal waters. At Sweet Bottom Dive Center, I rented a mask and fins, and went snorkeling among the parrotfish, angelfish, and wrasse that inhabit the shallow reef just offshore. After watching a sea turtle munch on seagrass, I flipped over onto my back. Above the beach the densely forested peaks of Maroon Country rose in layers, a physical reminder of the many lives and histories held within.

The Waves at Cane Bay, an 11-room boutique hotel built into the rocky shoreline overlooking the bay, was reimagined in 2021 as a stylish oceanfront retreat with private patios, two bars, and the sustainable seafood restaurant Ama. The hotel is a four-minute walk to the beach at Cane Bay and a nine-minute drive to the new Mount Eagle trailhead.

Located directly across the road from Cane Bay, the Landing Beach Bar serves up Caribbean specialties like jerk chicken and fried plantains in a fun, convivial setting. Leatherback Brewing Company is St. Croix's first craft brewery and an unofficial headquarters for the island's mountain-biking community, complete with a full-service bike shop inside.

#6256. United Pilots Squawk Hijack Code As Passenger Tries To Storm Cockpit, Says He Has A Bomb

A United Airlines flight from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport (MSY) took an eventful turn on Monday evening after a passenger reportedly tried to storm the cockpit. The alarming occurrence led the pilots to alert other United flights to the 'Level 4' threat, the most severe threat level indicating an attempted or actual breach of the cockpit, via the ACARS messaging system.

The flight ultimately landed safely in New Orleans. The response of the crew, which included issuing the squawk code 7500 to indicate unlawful interference, shows how seriously such threats are taken. It also comes just weeks after another United aircraft diverted following reports of a passenger threatening to hijack the plane.

United Airlines flight UA2174 is a regularly scheduled evening flight from Newark to New Orleans. On Monday, November 9, flight tracking data shows it departed Newark at 9:26 PM and touched down in New Orleans at 11:07 PM. However, during the flight, as flagged by FlightDeck on X, a male passenger tried to storm the Boeing 737 MAX 9's cockpit.

The pilots squawked 7500 to alert air traffic control to the threat, and later reported that he was carrying a backpack that he said contained a bomb. In an ACARS message to other United jets, they said:

"We had an attempted level four, no other details are known at this time."

7500 was first squawked as the jet descended through 20,000 feet, and it landed safely. Simple Flying reached out to United Airlines for further information on this incident, with a spokesperson confirming that there were 46 passengers and six members of crew on board. They added that:

"United flight 2174 from Newark to New Orleans landed safely following a disruptive incident involving a passenger onboard. Law enforcement met the aircraft upon arrival. "

By the time N17422 — the Boeing 737 MAX 9 operating United Airlines flight UA2174 — had arrived at its gate in New Orleans on Monday night, the passenger was said to be at the back of the aircraft, sitting with cabin crew. Few other details are known at this point. However, given the serious nature of his actions on board, police officers were likely waiting for him.

It was only last month that one of United's planes had to be diverted and locked down after a flight attendant spotted a passenger sending texts about hijacking the plane. In this instance, the jet was a Boeing 737 MAX 8 (as seen above) flying from Las Vegas to Newark.

With the suspicious messages spotted shortly after takeoff, the aircraft returned to Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), where it was met by law enforcement, rather than continuing to Newark. According to People, the texter, a 25-year-old male passenger, was under the influence of alcohol and was later arrested for making false threats regarding terrorism.

A Las Vegas flight turned back after cabin crew spotted a disturbing text and officers met the aircraft on return.

In recent times, 'squawk 7500' has become an increasingly common phrase in coverage of such alarming incidents as these. Arguably the most notable this year was the attempted hijacking of flydubai flight FZ1073 on its way from Dubai International Airport (DXB) to Tel Aviv Ben Gurion Airport (TLV). This flight issued the squawk codes 7700 and 7500, but what do they mean, and why are they so important?

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Squawk codes are essentially four-digit numbers that pilots can set their aircraft's transponder to in order to indicate their status to ATC. 7700 is used as a general emergency indicator, highlighting that a plane needs priority treatment. 7500 indicates a hijacking or unlawful interference, and it is a way of alerting ATC non-verbally without the hijackers knowing that controllers are aware of the situation.

#6255. Confused Air France Pilots Make Wrong Turn After Takeoff From LAX, Leading To Close Call

An Air France Airbus A350 departing from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) made a wrong turn after takeoff, sending the plane dangerously close to the path of an American Airlines Airbus A321. The way the pilots responded to this isn’t exactly great, though one thing is for sure — there seems to be a recurring problem involving runway 24L departures from the airport, whatever the cause may be.

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the audio and a visualization of an incident that happened shortly after 12AM on Saturday, November 7, 2026. It involves Air France flight AF28, which was operating to Papeete, French Polynesia (PPT).

LAX has four parallel runways, and the Air France A350 was cleared for takeoff on runway 24L, on the north side of the field. The Air France pilots were instructed to initially fly to the DLREY fix, instructions which they correctly read back.

Once through the DLREY fix, they were instructed to climb via their assigned SID (that they had received with clearance), but then the pilots suddenly made a turn to the left. The issue is that an American A321 had been cleared for takeoff on runway 25R just moments earlier, and that’s to the south of runway 24L.

So when the Air France pilots started turning to the left, they went directly into the path of the American plane. Fortunately the air traffic controller quickly caught this, but it created a traffic alert, and the planes had less than a mile of separation.

Mistakes happen, but what’s strange here is how this was handled after the initial incident. The air traffic controller asked the Air France pilots why they made a turn. The Air France pilot responded “standby,” which is fair enough. Pilots are supposed to be focused first on aviating, then on navigating, and then on communicating.

Moments later, the air traffic controller followed up and asked what departure the pilots had been instructed to fly. Once again, the pilot responded “standby one.” I do think the air traffic controller should’ve been a bit more patient here when a pilot is asking him to hold on for a second. At the same, the Air France pilots seemingly just kept stalling, and seemed to be unable to answer the question.

Of course we don’t know what was going on in the cockpit (it’s possible they were dealing with something else), but the controller wasn’t asking a complicated question. The pilots ended up getting a phone number for a possible pilot deviation.

It’s truly a mystery what caused the pilots to make that left turn, especially since they were flying to Tahiti, which is basically a straight westbound departure (and in the middle of the night, it’s not like you typically need to vector to the east when departing LAX).

Regardless of how good a system looks on paper, you of course have to consider human factors, and how systems are actually perceived. For reasons that are somewhat of a mystery, there seem to be repeated issues with planes departing from runway 24L at LAX making a turn to the left, and turning into the path of planes departing from runway 25R.

Just a couple of weeks ago, I covered how a TAP Air Portugal Airbus A330neo departing runway 24L at LAX made an unauthorized left turn immediately after takeoff, putting itself in the path of another jet.

Heck, just a couple of months ago, an Air France Boeing 777 departing runway 24L at LAX made an almost identical mistake, and turned left right after takeoff, when it wasn’t supposed to.

That’s only the tip of the iceberg in terms of the number of these incidents we’ve seen. I’m not sure what exactly is going on here, and if it’s a case of pilots programming their computers for a departure from runway 25R, only to get assigned runway 24L, or what.

But either way, it seems something should be done here. As redundant as it might sound when you’re sending pilots to a specific fix (which already tells them which direction they should go), it almost seems like air traffic control needs to add in a warning about not making a left turn without authorization. I mean, it sounds silly, but…

An Air France Airbus A350 departing LAX made an unauthorized left turn after takeoff, sending it right into the path of a departing American Airbus A321. The pilots really seemed to struggle with answering air traffic control’s basic questions, though I don’t know what was actually going on in the cockpit.

What’s so strange is how there seem to be repeated issues with departures from runway 24L, as we’ve now seen this “unauthorized left turn” situation from this exact runway several times in recent weeks alone.

What do you make of this LAX runway 24L issue?

#6254. Editor's Letter: Introducing Our Winter Travel Issue

It was a long and hot summer, and I welcomed the cooler weather as soon as the leaves started to turn. My closet full of coats and jackets had sat sadly neglected for many months; the new boots I bought in April on a clearance rack are only now about to get their moment. I'm excited for the Christmas lights in London and New York, the festive trees, chestnuts roasting on street corners—and yes, my Christmas wish list (featuring a dangerous number of watches and pieces of jewelry) is ready too. There is something about the winter that still feels exotic and enthralling to me. I saw snow a few times in Kashmir as a kid, but the first real blizzard I encountered was when I was a freshman in college in Pennsylvania. It was late at night, but my roommate dragged me out of bed to make snow angels. I still remember lying on my back, waving my arms around—the sensation of cold all along my body was surreal, as was the way in which white feathery bits floated down from the sky. I recall thinking, What a strange but wonderful feeling! I discovered two things quickly: One, I was a terrible skier. And, two, I loved après-ski—to be nursing hot chocolate by crackling fireplaces and snuggled in blankets.

Our story on Banff perfectly encapsulates the promise of winter: the adventure, the exhilaration, the romance of a landscape transformed overnight. But equally seductive is the prospect of winter sun. Come January I'll happily trade snow boots for sandals and fly to Tenerife, Spain, or Boracay, in the Philippines, or Brisbane, Australia. That dose of vitamin D is essential by then, when the Christmas lights have come down and everything seems gray and empty. At that point I need a beach—and something colorful and sparkly to wear on it. So often I close my eyes and return to the end-of-year trips I've made to Maldives, Indonesia, Mexico, and remembered the sunrises, the sound of the waves, the palm trees swaying in the breeze, the fiery red chiles, and fresh coconut water. It's been a strange year. But as we navigate the final months ahead, this issue is filled with reasons to feel excited about what comes next. I hope it gives you plenty to dream about—and somewhere to go.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6253. United Unveils 14-Gate Concourse at Dulles

United and the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority unveiled Washington Dulles International Airport’s first new concourse in nearly two decades on Monday. Concourse E opens to passengers Nov. 10, giving United 14 new gates at a hub where its departures have risen 30% since 2022.

The 435,000-square-foot concourse connects directly to the airport’s AeroTrain and has jet bridges at every gate. It can handle both domestic and international flights. The airports authority said existing gates were already fully in use several times a day, with passengers crowding waiting areas and concessions during peak periods.

The concourse also houses United’s second-largest United Club. The nearly 40,000-square-foot lounge seats more than 600 people and increases the airline’s total lounge space at Dulles by about 70%. New concessions include local businesses such as Good Company Doughnuts & Café and Honor Brewing.

“Washington Dulles is a critical part of United’s global network and growth strategy,” United CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement. The carrier currently offers more than 250 daily flights from Dulles to 135 destinations.

United has added six international destinations from the airport this year. It plans to begin international Airbus A321XLR service from Dulles in December with flights to Amsterdam and Dublin, followed by new service to Toulouse, France, and Milan in 2027.

Concourse E is the first phase of the broader Dulles Global Gateway program, which United and the airports authority estimate will involve more than $20 billion in investment. Later work is expected to add gates, expand the main terminal, and build a new U.S. Customs facility. The program also calls for extending the AeroTrain so the airport can eventually retire its mobile lounges.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

At The Points Guy, we’re always looking for simple ways to save money and earn more rewards. One of the easiest yet often overlooked tools is Chase Offers.

With just a few clicks, you can unlock targeted discounts and cash-back deals at brands you already use. These range from streaming services and restaurants to travel and retail purchases.

Even better, Chase Offers can often be combined with your card’s usual earning rates and shopping portals, helping you get more value from everyday spending.

Here’s how the program works and how to maximize it.

Chase Offers is a program available on eligible Chase debit and credit cards that gives cardholders access to targeted deals, similar to Amex Offers. These offers typically provide cash back or a percentage back as a statement credit when you make a qualifying purchase.

Like similar programs from other issuers, offers are personalized. That means the deals you see may differ from what someone else receives. You may also see different offers across your own Chase cards.

Most Chase-issued consumer and business credit and debit cards are eligible for Chase Offers if the primary cardholder has a U.S. address listed as their primary residence or place of business.

To see if Chase Offers is available for your card, check your Chase mobile app or log in at Chase's website.

For Chase credit cards, primary cardholders and authorized officers can view and add offers. Authorized users and employees can't add offers themselves, but they can redeem offers that have already been added to the account.

Some of the most popular eligible cards include:

Chase Offers are also available on many cobranded Chase credit cards, such as the (see rates and fees) and select United Airlines and Marriott Bonvoy cards.

Each card may offer different deals, so it's worth checking all your accounts if you hold more than one Chase card.

You can find available offers on the Chase website and on the Chase app. To view your available offers on the website, log in to your account and find "Chase Offers" on the right-hand panel.

Alternatively, you can click on "Benefits & travel" on the top panel and select "Chase Offers", as shown below. Note that the offers shown below may not be available to you.

To view your Chase Offers on the Chase mobile app, log in to your account and then scroll down toward the middle of the main account dashboard. You should see a section titled “Chase Offers” showing some of your current offers.

Either the website or app option will bring you to the offers currently available for you to browse.

Offerings change daily and typically feature various types of goods and services. You may see deals for:

Offers typically range from about 5% to 30% back or provide a fixed statement credit after meeting a spending requirement. For example, you might receive a $20 statement credit after spending $100 with a specific merchant.

Chase Offers can be an easy way to save on purchases you’re already making, which is something TPG staffers have seen firsthand across a range of everyday spending.

TPG travel writer Rachel Craft, for example, recently used an offer on her for 15% back at home improvement stores. She bundled supplies for a few projects she already had planned into a single purchase and received $33 back. Meanwhile, TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson earned an $85 statement credit on a DISH Network purchase using his World of Hyatt card.

TPG editor-in-chief Nick Ewen has also had success with Chase Offers. He recently earned $15.81 back on Trans-Siberian Orchestra tickets purchased through SeatGeek with his Chase Freedom Flex. Since the purchase also fell within one of the card's Q3 rotating quarterly bonus categories, he earned 5% cash back on top of his Chase Offer savings (on up to $1,500 in combined purchases each quarter, activation required).

And in an even bigger example of how these savings can add up, Nick earned a $125 statement credit through a Chase Offer on an IHG hotel stay booked through The Edit by Chase Travel℠, using his . By combining that offer with the card's The Edit and select hotels credits, he saved a total of $625 on the stay.

While individual savings may vary, these examples highlight how these targeted offers can add up, especially on purchases you already planned to make.

While you don’t have to enroll your card to start using the Chase Offers program, you do have to add each individual offer to your credit card. Adding them is easy — all you have to do is navigate to Chase Offers either online or through the Chase Mobile app and click “Add to card” on any available offer that interests you.

Alternatively, if you have a subscription to a service like MaxRewards Gold, your offers should be automatically activated for all linked cards.

Then, use your card at the specific merchant, and you should see a statement credit applied to your account within 30 days after your qualifying transaction posts, unless the offer terms state otherwise.

Once you arrive on the Chase Offers landing page, adding an offer to your account is very simple.

If you have multiple eligible Chase cards, you’ll see a “Choose your account” drop-down near the top of the screen. Note that if you have multiple sign-ins with Chase, such as one for your personal cards and one for business credit cards, you will only see cards associated with the account for which you’re currently signed in.

Again, note that the offers you see here may not be available for you.

Click on any offer to add it to your card. Then, use your card at the specific merchant and wait for your statement credit to post.

Once you find an offer you would like to use in the app, the process is similar to the website process.

You can click on “See all available deals” to see the rest of your offers. You’ll see a “Choose your account” drop-down near the top of the screen if you have multiple eligible Chase cards.

Click on any offers to add them to your card, use your card at the participating merchant and wait for your statement credit to post.

When you add an offer for a specific card, you must use that same card to redeem the offer. For example, if you add a Chase Offer to your , you must use that card to redeem that offer successfully.

Be sure to read the terms and conditions for each offer carefully. You only have a certain amount of time to use each offer, and many come with maximum earning limits. As long as you make your purchase by the expiration date, you should receive the credit even if the transaction posts after the expiration date.

Chase Offers are rewarded as a statement credit, even if you have a card that earns Ultimate Rewards points on regular spending.

One of the common threads among all Chase Offers is this condition: Payment must be made directly with the merchant. While you can still use services like mobile wallets and PayPal with Chase Offers, you can’t use third-party providers to make purchases.

Finally, Chase Offers are only available on eligible U.S.-issued Chase credit cards tied to U.S.-based accounts. However, some offers may still be valid at international merchants, particularly global brands like hotel chains, as long as the transaction is processed by the eligible merchant and charged to your enrolled card.

Since new offers are constantly added, it’s a good idea to go through your Chase Offers at least biweekly to review and add new offers. It doesn’t cost anything to add an offer and then not use it, so you can be pretty lenient with which offers you add.

If there’s even a tiny possibility that you’ll use an offer, you might as well add it to your card. If you use it, great; if not, it’s not a problem.

Chase Offers become significantly more valuable when you stack them with other rewards opportunities. This means combining an offer with a shopping portal and a credit card bonus category to earn multiple layers of rewards on the same purchase.

For example, imagine you’re booking a $200 stay at a Hyatt property. You could:

In this scenario, you’d earn 1,000 points through the portal, $10 cash back from your Freedom Flex and a $20 statement credit from the Chase Offer.

Instead of earning rewards from just one source, you’ve effectively tripled up on the same purchase.

Chase Offers are best used for purchases you were already planning to make. Like any coupon or sale, saving 10% on something you didn’t need isn’t actually saving money. But when used strategically, especially in combination with shopping portals and bonus categories, they can meaningfully boost your overall return.

*Earn 5% cash back in rotating categories for the first $1,500 in combined purchases each quarter; activation required.

Chase Offers is one of the easiest ways to save money on purchases you already plan to make. While the discounts may not always be large, they require minimal effort and can add up quickly.

By checking your offers regularly and combining them with bonus categories and shopping portals, you can turn everyday spending into meaningful savings over time.

#6251. Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card Review: Worth The $95 Fee For The Free Night

Marriott has co-branded credit cards issued by both American Express and Chase, and it can be tough to figure out the differences between these cards. This is my review of the most popular mid-range Marriott credit card in that portfolio, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card. It’s a card that many Marriott guests will likely want to have, if eligible.

Let’s dive into the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card’s details to see whether it’s worth it and who it makes the most sense for.

Link: Learn more about the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card

Before I get into my full Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card review, here’s a brief look at the card’s key details:

I also put together my list of pros and cons for the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card:

To start, let’s take a look at the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card welcome bonus, card eligibility rules, and fees. After all, these are important factors that cardmembers consider when applying for cards. Now is an especially good time to apply, thanks to the current offer.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is currently offering a multi-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn three free night awards. The bonus is broken down as follows:

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each, given all the great ways there are to redeem them. While the maximum value of this offer is 150,000 points, I wouldn’t value the bonus quite that high, given the limited flexibility (you need to redeem the free night award within a year, you’re capped at properties costing 50,000 points, etc.).

However, if it were worth 150,000 points, I’d consider that to have a value of $1,050, and that doesn’t factor in the potential airline statement credits.

If you’re applying for the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, the general Chase application restrictions apply. There aren’t too many direct, consistent rules, but considerations include Chase’s 5/24 rule (which isn’t always enforced), being able to get up to two Chase cards every 30 days, etc.

Beyond that, since both American Express and Chase issue cards for Marriott, there are some pretty complicated restrictions regarding eligibility for this card, so see this post for more details.

To summarize the very basics, you can’t get the welcome bonus on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card if:

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card has a $95 annual fee. You can add authorized users at no extra cost. That’s an incredibly reasonable annual fee, given the amount of annual fee inflation we’ve seen over the years on other cards.

The Bonvoy Boundless Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s an excellent card for purchases abroad. That means you can earn rewards on your foreign spending, without having to pay any fees that will offset those rewards. In particular, it’s a good card to use for foreign Marriott spending.

While I wouldn’t recommend using the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card for your everyday spending, there are potentially some situations where it could make sense. Let’s go over the rewards structure of the card, including the bonus categories and other incentives to spend.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 6x Bonvoy points for spending at Marriott-family hotels globally. For many people, this will be a worthwhile bonus.

Since I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, that’s the equivalent of a 4.2% return on hotel spending. While there are other great cards for hotel spending, some people will want to use this as their card for Marriott spending.

Keep in mind this is on top of the standard points that you can earn for Marriott Bonvoy hotel stays. At most brands, Bonvoy members earn 10x points per dollar spent, and that’s before elite bonuses, which range from 10-75%. So as a Bonvoy Silver member paying with the card (the minimum status you get with this card), you’re looking at earning 17x points per dollar spent at most brands, minimum.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 3x Bonvoy points on dining, gas station, and grocery store purchases globally. This only applies to the first $6,000 spent on combined purchases in those categories annually, and after that, you’ll earn 2x Bonvoy points on those purchases.

Since I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, the 3x points is like the equivalent of a 2.1% return on eligible gas, grocery, and dining spending. While there are still more rewarding cards for spending in the categories of dining, gas stations, and groceries, this is about as good of a rewards structure as you’ll see on a Bonvoy credit card.

The Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 2x Bonvoy points on all other eligible purchases. I don’t consider 2x points per dollar spent to be especially compelling since I value that at a return of 1.4 cents per dollar of spending, and there are better cards for everyday spending.

How would I approach the value of Marriott points? As mentioned above, based on my valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each. I’m not going to suggest that Bonvoy points are my favorite points currency — they’re not — but the reality is that Marriott has a huge global portfolio, and many of the properties are quite decent.

Generally you’ll find that Bonvoy award stays cost anywhere from 10,000 to 200,000 points per night, though some hotels do fall outside of that range. You can maximize value by taking advantage of the fifth night free benefit, which is open to elite members.

This is an extreme example of value, but take Hotel Cala di Volpe, a Marriott Luxury Collection hotel in Sardinia, which is the brand’s most expensive property in summer. I just pulled up a five night redemption (including a fifth night free) for 776,000 Bonvoy points. By my valuation, that’s like $5,432 worth of points.

Meanwhile the cash rate at the hotel is 4,161 EUR ($4,639) per night, so those same five nights would cost you $23,195. Talk about huge savings!

One unique thing about Bonvoy points is they can also fairly efficiently be converted into airline miles. You can transfer your rewards to dozens of different airline programs, and a vast majority allow a 3:1 transfer ratio. On top of that, you get a bonus of 5,000 airline miles for every 60,000 Bonvoy points you transfer. In other words, with most programs you can convert 60,000 Bonvoy points into 25,000 airline miles, which is potentially a decent value.

For more details, see my guide to redeeming Bonvoy points.

One of the primary reasons to consider getting the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is how the card can help you earn elite status in the Bonvoy program. Status starts to get valuable around the Bonvoy Platinum tier, when you become eligible for perks like complimentary breakfast and valuable room upgrades.

One of my favorite perks of having the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is that you get 15 elite nights toward status annually just for having the card.

Note that several co-branded Marriott credit cards offer this, and you can only receive the benefit once per year on a personal card. In other words, if you have three Marriott personal cards, then you wouldn’t get 45 elite nights.

However, you could earn 15 elite nights from this personal card and 15 elite nights from a business card, so that you’d earn 30 elite nights in a year. The ideal setup would be to have a personal card in conjunction with the Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more).

This makes it more attainable to earn Platinum status, which requires 50 elite nights. If you had the Bonvoy Boundless Card, you’d only need 35 more elite nights, and if you also had the business card you’d only need 20 more elite nights.

Note that if you really want to maximize elite nights with personal credit cards, the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) offers 25 elite nights per year, which is the most elite nights you’ll get with any Marriott credit card.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers one elite night for every $5,000 spent on the card. Any elite nights earned this way will be credited to your account within eight weeks of the last day of the calendar month in which you qualify.

Personally, I think spending $5,000 to earn one elite night is a lot, but everyone’s situation will differ, and for some people, this could make sense if you’re otherwise close to earning status. This is the only Marriott credit card that offers bonus elite nights for spending.

Perhaps this is a bit redundant, but just for having the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card you receive Silver elite status in the Bonvoy program. Now, don’t get too excited, as this doesn’t exactly come with that many benefits.

Marriott Silver elite status ordinarily requires 10 elite nights, and comes with perks like 10% bonus points on hotel stays, priority late check-out, and free Wi-Fi. So it’s better than nothing, but that’s about all I can say.

If you have the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, you can earn Marriott Gold elite status if you spend $35,000 on the card in a calendar year. This status ordinarily requires 25 elite nights. Bonvoy Gold elite status gets you benefits like 25% bonus points on hotel stays, 2PM late check-out, a room upgrade subject to availability, and more.

In addition to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card spending bonus categories and ability to earn elite status, there are some other major perks to having the card. This is where the card’s annual fee becomes really easy to justify, in my opinion.

The real perk that makes the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card worthwhile is that you get a free night award every year on your account anniversary, valid for a one-night hotel stay at a property costing up to 35,000 points.

It’s also possible to top off Marriott free night awards with up to 25,000 additional points to redeem at more expensive properties. This means you could redeem a free night award plus 25,000 points to stay at a hotel costing 60,000 points per night.

This is an exceptional deal, and I think this card is worth having. Marriott is the world’s largest hotel chain, so regardless of your preferred hotel program, just about everyone may find themselves in a situation where this could come in handy.

I consistently redeem this certificate at hotels costing $250+ per night. Based on my valuation of 0.7 cents per point, I’d consider the free night award to be worth around $245, more than double the annual fee… that’s awesome!

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers auto rental collision damage waiver coverage. Decline the rental company’s collision insurance and charge the entire rental cost to your card.

Coverage is provided for theft and collision damage for most cars in the United States and abroad. Do note that within the United States, coverage is secondary to your personal insurance, though. Of course you’ll always want to check the guide to benefits for all the details.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers a variety of protection when traveling. Among these features are:

Make sure you check your cardmember agreement and guide to benefits for all of the details, since there are terms to be aware of.

Personally, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card isn’t a card that I would be using for my everyday spending. However, I think the card is worth having, given that it offers a free night certificate on your account anniversary every year, which should more than justify the annual fee.

If you’re going for status, the 15 elite nights toward status annually is incredibly valuable as well, and makes it easier to earn Platinum status.

I think there’s absolutely merit to picking up the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, though I’d say that the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) might be the best alternative to consider. While the card is issued by American Express and has a steep $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees), there are lots of reasons to consider this card, including:

Obviously this card won’t be for everyone, and the fee is steep. However, I do think the perks add up, and if you’re involved quite a bit in the Bonvoy ecosystem, it’s easy to make the math on the card work.

If you’re not actually that committed to the Marriott Bonvoy ecosystem, there are lots of other great cards to consider. In particular, these are cards with relatively reasonable annual fees and great rewards structures, and they’re very well rounded:

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is a great card with a reasonable annual fee, and offers an annual free night award and 15 elite nights toward status annually. This is an especially good time to apply, given the welcome offer that’s currently available.

#6250. Air France Takes Its 60th A220 as A318s Fly On

Air France took delivery of its 60th Airbus A220-300 on Friday, completing the order it placed in 2019 to replace its A318s, A319s and some A320s. The airline’s remaining A318s are still scheduled to fly through March 27, 2027.

The new A220, registered F-HOZJ and named Mimizan, arrived just over five years after Air France put the type into commercial service in October 2021. The airline says its 148-seat A220s now serve 50 destinations and have carried nearly 24 million passengers.

Air France had initially expected to have all 60 A220s in its fleet by 2025. The carrier has also pushed back the end of A318 flying. An August schedule update moved the last planned flights from Nov. 8 to March 27, according to AeroRoutes. The winter schedule includes A318 service from Paris Charles de Gaulle to destinations such as Barcelona, Dublin, and Rome.

Air France took delivery of its first A318 − the smallest A320 family variant − in October 2003 and went on to operate 18, the largest fleet of the type. Three remain active, according to fleet data from Planespotters.net.

The 60th delivery closes out the initial firm order, which also included 30 options and 30 purchase rights. Air France says its 61st A220 and subsequent deliveries will have Wi-Fi installed before entering commercial service. About 85% of the A220s already in service have the equipment, with the remaining installations due by February 2027.

#6249. The Airlines With The World's Newest Premium Economy Seats In 2026

Around the world, premium economy is growing and more airlines are expected to increase their capacity in this class, although it can take years for an airline to fully transition to a new cabin type. Broadly speaking, premium economy is confined to widebody aircraft assigned to longer-haul routes.

However, there are exceptions like American Airlines' transcontinental A321XLRs and Emirates' widebodies that are used for short-haul routes. Widebodies generally fall into three categories as far as rolling out a new seating class is concerned. One category is new aircraft being delivered, which are typically received from the manufacturer with the latest airline cabins.

Another group of aircraft is those already in service with years of service ahead of them. These are retrofitted as they are cycled through their scheduled maintenance. Finally, there are older aircraft in service that are scheduled to retire that an airline may not bother retrofitting.

Originally, all commercial fares were effectively first class, as flying was only something the elite could afford to do. Over time, economy class emerged, and then in the 1970s, business class emerged as a bridge between first and economy. For many business class passengers, first class was excessively expensive, while economy was not befitting of business representatives on business trips.

The class also introduced the notion of working on the aircraft. As air travel became mainstream and everyone could fly, flying lost its prestige status symbol. Private jets may be the domain of the wealthy, but not commercial flying, and no longer did passengers dress up for the occasion and treat it as something of a first-class voyage.

Without the status of the past, the first class became seen as excessively expensive, while also being squeezed by an improving business class. This has led to the decline of first class around the world. Meanwhile, pressures mounted in two directions. One was the increased demand for ultra-cheap and utilitarian flights, which gave rise to low-cost and ultra-low-cost carriers.

Another was the demand for a class better than economy, but not as prohibitively expensive as business class. This led to the rise of premium economy as a 'sweet spot' between affordability and comfort. It fits today's mainline market, where flying needs to be comfortable and affordable, but not overly lavish.

Premium economy is the youngest of the four classes, and many airlines were reluctant to introduce it. Some airlines saw it as a threat that would undermine their profitable business class, as premium economy works if it gets economy-class passengers to upgrade, but it is counterproductive if it convinces business-class passengers to downgrade.

Some mainline carriers, like Emirates, were also concerned about how it would affect their brand image as a luxury mainline airline. Now, however, that dam has burst, and airlines are rushing to retrofit their aircraft with premium economy. Emirates CEO Tim Clark said that "our Premium Economy product was carefully developed in keeping with Emirates’ brand positioning as a full-service airline of the highest quality."

Industry Standards For Premium Economy (Per Emirates)

Cost above the economy (varies regionally)

Business cost above premium (varies regionally)

He has also described the demand for Emirates' premium economy as "tremendous" and "shocking" while noting he could sell the seats multiple times. Emirates is a great example of a holdout that has now fully embraced the class.

In 2026, Emirates has not been introducing a new premium economy, as it already exists, but it is rolling it out for more and more routes as aircraft are retrofitted, such as Tokyo to Cairo via Dubai. Lufthansa has gone so far as to call it a "money-generating machine" and claim it generates 33% more per square foot than economy class and 6% more than business class.

While Emirates has its own official Premium Economy, both Qatar and Etihad have their own unique approach to an elevated economy experience.

United Airlines is upgrading its Boeing 787-9's international cabins with a refreshed premium economy class as part of its broader 'Elevated Interior' launch. In May 2025, the carrier said that "United expects to take delivery of the first 787-9 with the Elevated interior before the end of 2025, ​​​​​ with the first international passenger flights planned in 2026 from San Francisco to Singapore and San Francisco to London."

American Airlines' new premium economy debuted in late 2025 on its new Being 787-9 Dreamliners (789P) and A321XLR transcontinental aircraft, while existing 777-300ERs are being retrofitted with the new seats. This is part of American's cabin refresh, and it is the last US-based airline to finally ditch first class, while it rebalances with more premium economy options.

Delta Air Lines is enhancing its premium economy class at the expense of economy class seats, while JetBlue is introducing its Junior Mint seats in 2026. While not typically classified as traditional premium economy, Junior Mint is still presented as a bridge between economy and business.

One holdout appeared to be Alaska Airlines. Its Hawaiian-bound Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners were initially only configured with business and economy class. However, it announced in October that, from 2028, 787s, A330s, and select 737 MAX 10s will get "international-grade premium economy with 38 inches of pitch, leg and calf rests and 16-inch 4K screens."

In Europe, Virgin Atlantic is taking delivery of new A330neo aircraft with expanded premium cabins (56). Elsewhere, Lufthansa is now accepting its new Boeing 787 Dreamliners after delays with the new Allegris cabins, while more A350-900s with Allegris premium economy cabins are delivered. Older Lufthansa aircraft, like 747-8s, are to be retrofitted.

In December 2025, Business Travel News Europe reported that "TAP Air Portugal in summer 2026 will introduce a new premium economy cabin on long-haul flights for its Airbus A330 and A321LR aircraft." It added that this will include 12 seats in three rows of four on these narrowbody aircraft. British Airways is also in the process of refreshing its cabin interiors, including its premium economy seats.

By now, the vast majority of major European full-service airlines with significant long-haul networks have adopted premium economy. However, there are a few holdouts, most notably Ireland's Aer Lingus, Spain's Air Europa, and, until now, Turkish Airlines. Turkish Airlines is, however, relaunching its premium economy after a lengthy hiatus on long-haul flights in 2028.

The refreshed premium economy seats are more comfortable, aesthetically pleasing, and technologically advanced than older seats.

EVA Air unveiled its fourth-generation premium economy seats in early 2025. As a side point, EVA Air is widely credited for having launched the world's first true premium economy class in 1992, which, at the time, was called Evergreen Deluxe. Singapore Airlines and Air France are also among the airlines rolling out refreshed premium economy seats in 2026.

Philippine Airlines has unveiled its first Airbus A350-1000 with a premium economy cabin, and more of these aircraft have arrived in 2026. As stated, one of the biggest stories for premium economy is Emirates, which is estimated to be adding 10 more premium economy routes, bringing the total to over 84. It is rolling out premium across its refreshed Boeing 777s and A380s, while, as a first, its new A350-900s are not being delivered with first class seats in favor of premium economy.

Air New Zealand is among the airlines doubling down on premium economy, introducing increased premium economy capacity on its retrofitted Boeing 787 Dreamliners from late 2025 into 2026. The carrier stated in mid-2025 that "customers travelling to North America will have access to more than 34,000 additional seats, alongside a boost of 20,500 premium seats across the wider long-haul network."

Elsewhere, Thai Airways has plans to add a new premium economy cabin to its 777-300ERs and incoming 787-9s starting around 2027. Meanwhile, new premium economy announcements in 2025 included LATAM saying it would introduce a new Premium Comfort cabin on its Boeing 787-8 and 787-9 starting in 2027.

Premium economy is now the fastest-growing class, having grown by 8% in recent years, ahead of economy's 5.9% growth. In 2027, Germany's leisure carrier, Discover Airlines, is introducing a premium economy cabin known as 'Ocean Blue' on its A330 widebody fleet. flydubai is also adding premium economy for the first time on its new Boeing 787 Dreamliners in 2027.

In contrast, first class seating is down by around 40% compared with 2019. In Q4 of 2025, Delta Air Lines reached a new milestone, as premium cabin revenue exceeded economy revenue. The final quarter saw main cabin revenues fall by 7% from $6 billion to $5.6 billion.

Meanwhile, premium revenues jumped by almost the same amount for the quarter ($473 million), from $5.2 billion in 2024 to $5.7 billion in 2025. Overall, the full-year main economy cabin revenues exceeded those of the premium economy cabin, but it seems that 2025 was the tipping point for Delta.

#6248. In Winter, Canada's Banff National Park is So Much More Than a Skiers' Paradise

My view from the foot of gleaming Victoria Glacier was straight out of a snow globe. Two shaggy ebony draft horses pulled a vintage sleigh along a powdery path that hugged the shores of frozen Lake Louise. Lycra-clad Nordic skiers glided across the snow-dusted ice, navigating around life-size snowmen. In the far distance a ray of sun glinted off the turret of an ice-sculpted castle, a mini version of the grand Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise hotel, which stands sentinel over this unbelievably pretty patch of wilderness in Banff National Park. A soft gust of wind swirled a flurry of flakes across the scene. The winter wonderland in front of me was magical enough to make even the most die-hard snowbirds reconsider the season.

I've always felt winter could be approached in two ways: You could be lazy and binge Netflix for three months, or you could be sporty and get after it in the mountains. But a weeklong trip to the Banff and Lake Louise region of Alberta opened my eyes to a gratifying middle ground. This area is a true winter playground, where you could downhill-ski or engage with the elements in so many other ways: snowshoeing, going for a horse-drawn sleigh ride, or watching the snowflakes fall while you're soaking in an outdoor hot tub. My time ended up being more about appreciating nature than conquering it on the slopes.

A seat with a view inside Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise

I arrived in early January on the tail of one of the area's snowiest Decembers on record, though you couldn't tell from the landscape around Calgary airport. Umber-hued prairies and agricultural land surround the gateway city, and it wasn't until 40 minutes into my 90-minute drive west on the Trans-Canada Highway that the Great Plains transitioned to the Canadian Rockies and the sky started nuking snow.

Home to SkiBig3—a trio of resorts that include Banff Sunshine, Lake Louise Ski Resort, and the mom-and-pop Mount Norquay—Banff National Park was the place to be during a winter in which most of the American West suffered a snow drought. In my 20s I would have driven straight from the airport to the ski slopes. Now in my mid-40s, with an unpredictable knee, back-to-back, bell-to-bell days have lost their appeal. But the childlike joy of playing in the snow has not. And Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise was the perfect base for “soft” winter adventure.

The resort's address, in the heart of Banff National Park overlooking glacier-fed Lake Louise, envelops guests in nature. No surprise—Lake Louise was originally developed for outdoor tourism. In 1885, after the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway was driven in, future company president William Cornelius Van Horne built hotels along the route. Among the first, the Banff Springs Hotel was designed for horseback sightseeing. The Chalet at Lake Louise, a humble log cabin, was marketed as a destination for fishing, canoeing, and alpinism. Van Horne hired Swiss guides to teach his guests to safely navigate the mountains, and they are partially responsible for introducing locals to the sport of skiing.

A horse-drawn sleigh ride around Lake Louise

In 1925 the original Chalet, which had been damaged in a fire, was reimagined as Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise, a grand, Renaissance Revival–style resort with 539 rooms and suites. Today, a century after opening, some characteristics—like its staff dressed in lederhosen-inspired uniforms and its fondue-focused restaurant, Walliser Stube—nod to the original Swiss influence, and the lobby-level Guide's Cabin, decorated with vintage photos and stocked with books on alpine living, continues the property's mountaineering legacy. Through the hotel, guests can sign up for snowshoe hikes or Bavarian curling lessons and rent ice skates and Nordic skis.

My first morning, I met guide Kevin Kirkpatrick at the cabin for an activity called Powderfest Snowshoeing. I've long found snowshoeing a little snoozy and worried how we'd fill the allotted three hours. The activity's name, it turned out, wasn't a cutesy marketing ploy. The resort has seven snowshoe trails, but because there was a base of 61 inches and another foot of fresh powder, we went “off-roading.”

Leaving behind the groomed lakeshore trail, we trekked up the shoulder of Fairview Mountain, and all signs of civilization disappeared as we entered a frosted forest straight out of a Dr. Seuss story. “Really get in there and explore,” he encouraged as we wandered past fir and larch trees bent at cartoonish angles, their limbs heaving with snow. I followed him up a massive mound of powder only to catch the metal cleat of my snowshoe on a branch and topple backward, leaving an imprint like a gigantic snow angel.

Time flew as Kirkpatrick shared wisdom on everything from the current weather anomaly to how, in 1882, Edwin Hunter, a member of the Stoney Nakoda, first led a young European wrangler, Tom Wilson, to what the Indigenous people of this area called Ho-run-num-nay (Lake of the Little Fishes). He chose to ignore the name and anointed it Emerald Lake for its jewel-colored waters. Two years later the government changed the moniker to Louise to honor a daughter of Queen Victoria, Princess Louise Caroline Alberta.

An ice climber on the Lake Louise Lakeshore Trail

I returned to the hotel thoroughly exhausted from hours of high-stepping and grateful that I was booked for a session at Basin Glacial Waters, Fairmont's new, guests-only thermal bathhouse. Designed by Italian architect Matteo Thun, the building, with floor-to-ceiling windows that frame the lake and towering peaks at every turn, feels like part of the landscape. This is the epitome of nature bathing, I thought as I took in the views from the hot-stone room, silent salt chamber, and indoor-outdoor vitality pool.

I didn't think it was possible to distract me from the dramatic vista, but Basin's signature Aufguss sauna ritual, the conclusion to my multisensory journey, was impossible to ignore. This choreographed sauna performance popular across Europe has only recently been introduced to North American spas. For 15 minutes our sauna master, Kyan Van Haasteren, a young, blond Dutchman, theatrically waved a towel over scorching sauna stones to waft steam toward me and 32 other guests. He danced around the 185-degree-Fahrenheit space to an upbeat soundtrack of Luis Fonsi while smashing snowballs scented with aromatic oils over the hot stones to release the fragrance of Siberian fir. It felt more like a Vegas show than a wellness ritual, but the entertainment took my mind off the discomfort of the heat. I exited in a sweaty daze and willed myself to follow Van Haasteren's lead and dunk myself into the outdoor cold plunge. In seconds the tingling numbness gave way to a heady euphoria. I looked up to see the start of a steady snow spiraling down, one that wouldn't let up until late the next day.

I may not be a first-to-last-chair skier any longer, but I'm still motivated to score fresh tracks on a powder day. By 8 a.m. the next morning, I was on the complimentary Fairmont shuttle with a throng of stoked skiers for the 10-minute transfer to Lake Louise Ski Resort. With three ways up the front of the mountain, there's rarely a line. And once you're on the mountain, it's easy to spread out. With this season's addition of Richardson's Ridge, 200 acres of beginner- and intermediate-friendly glades and groomers, the resort owns bragging rights as the third biggest ski area in Canada, with 4,200 acres of skiable terrain. Throughout the day I experienced moments that felt more like backcountry than resort riding, especially in the rowdy inbounds steeps of the West Bowl.

Gearing up to snowshoe at Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise

I spent the morning lapping bowl runs off the Summit Chair, but in the afternoon the visibility disappeared, making a drop down black diamond Rodney's Ridge downright vertigo-inducing. I'd gotten my fix of SkiBig3's “Prosecco Powder” (wonderfully light, dry snow), and I won't lie—the other incentive that got me up and out early was the promise of lunch at Whitehorn Bistro. The acclaimed views from this upscale, on-mountain restaurant were obscured, but that didn't damper the deliciousness of its farm-to-table dishes, like pickled beet carpaccio with goat cheese and crispy duck with black cherry jus.

With a solid half day of riding under my belt, I left the resort to work off my lunch on the Nordic trails of the Lake Louise campground with Clare McCann, the high-energy owner of Bikescape. Her lighthearted guiding philosophy was an ideal match for my novice cross-country ski skills and the tricky conditions. Heavy wet snow would cement our skis to the ground the minute we stopped propelling forward. “Shimmy, shimmy, shimmy, glide,” she repeated like a mantra as we haltingly made our way around the four-mile Bow River Loop. The trail was so silent that the only sound was my retro SkiBig3 pass flapping on the side of my jacket.

Those words stuck with me as I drove 50 minutes southeast to the town of Banff. Compared with Lake Louise, it's a bustling tourism hub, but thanks to strict design guidelines, the businesses downtown—even the Starbucks and the McDonald's—are housed in intentionally rustic spaces built from local stone and wood. Over the last few years, new businesses have enlivened the downtown area. Some of these arrivals include locavore-focused restaurants Good Folk and Farm & Fire, and the 67-room boutique Kenrick Hotel, a hip remodel of the former High Country Inn that added a third-wave coffee shop, a thermal circuit spa, and a stellar Italian restaurant, The Fat Ox. Even the classic sticky-floored late-night club, the Dusty Boot Saloon & Dance Hall, has been reinvented as Banff's take on Jackson Hole's Million Dollar Cowboy Bar, complete with a shiny, boot-shaped disco ball and a karaoke room.

I kept things old-school and checked in to Fairmont Banff Springs, nicknamed the Castle in the Rockies for its Scottish-baronial-style architecture and perch overlooking the town. The hotel was another vision of railway executive Van Horne, who famously said, “If we can't export the scenery, we'll import the tourists.”

Today Banff National Park sees more than 4.25 million visitors every year; nearly two thirds come during summer. But a week into my trip, I began to think that winter might be the more enchanting season. On my final day I joined Discover Banff Tours on an excursion to Johnston Canyon for its Icewalk experience. In the parking lot our guide, Jeff Doherty, outfitted our group of six in Yaktrax—ice-gripping cleats that attach to shoes—then had us briskly hike a half mile over slick paths and bridges to the lower falls before the big bus tour groups arrived.

The canyon was pure quietude, and we had it to ourselves. When the pace slowed, I was able to admire the feathery moss suspended in frost on the forest floor, the icy old man's beard lichen dangling from the trees, and, most of all, the frozen ribbons of electric blue cascades. About a mile of slippery uphill trail led us to the upper falls, a stream of water plunging behind a veil of ice. I stood in front of Mother Nature's ice sculpture in awe. “It's like seeing the Mona Lisa alone in the Louvre,” said Doherty. “In summer you'd be elbowing iPhones out of the way for a view, let alone a photo.”

A few weeks after I'd returned home to Colorado, I read that Alberta had been hit by a warm spell that doused the mountains in rain, turning the slopes into sheets of ice. Some friends had taken their family on a ski trip per my recommendation. When I asked about their vacation, they told me they hadn't skied once, but they had the best time dogsledding, night tubing, and ice-skating. In an age when weather is unforgivingly unpredictable, Banff, with its buffet of activities, might be the closest thing to a guaranteed winter escape, no matter your preferred pace of adventure. My trip showed me that winter isn't just about high-voltage powder days at the ski resort. It can be enjoyed at a slower pace. I was even inspired to buy a pair of my own snowshoes.

Direct flights to Calgary International Airport are available from more than a dozen major US hubs. Banff National Park is an easy 90-minute drive west on the Trans-Canada Highway.

Lakefront grande dame Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise offers every imaginable snowy activity, from horse-drawn sleigh rides to curling. In winter an outdoor bar built from 240 blocks of ice serves mulled wine and spiked cocoa. Only hotel guests have access to Basin Glacial Waters, a sprawling thermal bathhouse. Don't miss the excellent hotel bookshop, curated with out-of-print editions on the area's mountaineering history.

One of the park's first hotels, Fairmont Banff Springs, recently added a new wing of larger, family-friendly suites with bunk beds and adjoining rooms. An on-site skating rink has a pop-up sugar shack that serves maple treats, and the adventure center rents fat-tire bikes and arranges guided evening snowshoe tours. Of the 13 dining venues, 1888 Chophouse, known for its Alberta Wagyu, is a standout.

A refreshing boutique alternative to Banff's palatial resorts, the reimagined Kenrick Hotel has an outpost of Calgary's Analog Coffee, a guests-only hydrotherapy spa that stays open until midnight, and one of the town's top tables, Alpine Italian–inspired Fat Ox.

Tucked away on Sulphur Mountain, 320-room resort Rimrock Banff, Emblems Collection debuted a sleek makeover last summer. The first property in Accor's new über-luxe Emblems Collection features a bathhouse of saunas, glacial plunges, and infinity pools, plus a cocktail-forward vinyl listening room and in-house guides who can take guests on glacier treks and ice canyon walks.

Reservations are a must at white-tablecloth Dining Room at the Post Hotel and Spa, known for its 25,000-plus-bottle wine cellar and European-inspired menu of dishes like roasted chateaubriand and Dover sole with saffron beurre blanc.

The house-made sourdough alone makes it worth pausing on a powder day for lunch at ski-in, ski-out restaurant Whitehorn Bistro off the Grizzly Gondola of Lake Louise Ski Resort. On a bluebird day request a patio seat.

The Dusty Boot Saloon and Dance Hall was recently spiffed up and turned into an Old West saloon with a stage for live music and a menu of excellent cocktails, like the Cattleman's Old Fashioned, and elevated bar food, including addictive popcorn chicken and shrimp spiked with wasabi peas.

At Good Folk, hearty breakfast dishes like banana caramel French toast will fuel your day's adventure. In the evening the menu showcases the local bounty in dishes like Alberta wild boar chop and a decadent bison burger topped with smoked cheddar and pepper bacon.

Johnston Canyon, a labyrinth of limestone rocks and cascades, sees a fraction of the visitors in winter than in summer. But to make sure you have the frozen falls to yourself, book the morning Icewalk experience with Discover Banff Tours.

Local outfitter Bikescape runs beginner-friendly Nordic ski tours on the trails within Banff National Park as well as electric fat-tire bike tours that include a backcountry lunch.

Sit back and enjoy the views of Lake Louise from the seat of a horse-drawn sled. Brewsters Lake Louise Stables runs hour-long trips that follow the lake path; evening tours under the stars are extra special.

SkiBig3's resorts offer something for everyone. Family-friendly Mount Norquay has night skiing and a thrilling tubing park. Every chairlift on the front side of Lake Louise Ski Resort has both an easy (green) and challenging (black) way down. Sunshine Mountain Lodge at Banff Sunshine Village has the area's only ski-in, ski-out lodging, and its big alpine views make you feel like you're downhilling in Europe.

For the perfect detour en route to Calgary International Airport, Everwild Canmore, a new Nordic spa at the Everwild hotel in the town of Canmore, features a DIY outdoor thermal circuit as well as five-elements rituals, ranging from an herbal steam cleanse to an Aufguss ceremony. The spa lounge serves a shareable charcuterie and cheese board for two along with cocktails.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
